answer:
**Pie chart**: it shows parts of one whole, and angles are hard to compare across
categories; bar and column charts are the standard comparison charts. (The first two
options are under the selection bar and are read as Bar Graph and Pie Chart.)

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: year closest to the twenty-year average
stem:
A company's revenue (in Cr) for 2001-2020 was 93, 95, 100, 105, 108, 109, 110, 120, 125,
130, 132, 134, 140, 145, 150, 150, 155, 160, 160, 180. Which year's revenue equals
(approximately) the average of the twenty years?
answer: **(c) 2010**: the total is 2601, the average 130.05, and 2010 had 130.

subject: Machine learning
title: Q2, generalisation gap
stem:
Let $L_{val}$ and $L_{train}$ denote the loss on validation data and training data. The
generalisation gap is $L_{gap} = L_{val} - L_{train}$. If $L_{gap} \gg 0$, what does it
denote?
answer:
**(a) Overfitting.** The model does much better on the data it was trained on
than on unseen data, so it has memorised the training set. Underfitting shows up as a
*high training* loss, with a small gap.

subject: Machine learning
title: Q3, convolution output shape
stem:
What is the shape of the output activation map when an input image of shape
$32 \times 32 \times 3$ is convolved with 6 filters of shape $5 \times 5$?
answer:
\textbf{(b) $28 \times 28 \times 6$.} With stride 1 and no padding each spatial size is
$32 - 5 + 1 = 28$; each filter (implicitly $5 \times 5 \times 3$) gives one output
channel, so 6 channels.

subject: Machine learning
title: Q4, softmax confidence
stem:
Image classification with 5 classes $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$: the output logits of the
model for one image are $[3.2, 5.1, 0.8, 2.2, 3.9]$. What is the confidence of the model
in its prediction (softmax output)?
answer:
**(a) 65.82%.** The prediction is class 1 (largest logit), with confidence
$e^{5.1} / \sum_k e^{z_k} = 164.0 / 249.2 = 0.6582$. (Checked numerically; the full
softmax is $[0.098, 0.658, 0.009, 0.036, 0.198]$.) Tip: subtract the largest logit
first, $e^{0} / (e^{-1.9} + 1 + e^{-4.3} + e^{-2.9} + e^{-1.2})$, which is easier by hand.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q5, three friends and rain
stem:
Three friends in Tokyo tell you that it is rainy. Each person has a probability of
$1/4$ of lying. What is the probability that it is raining in Tokyo? Assume
$P(\text{rain}) = 1/5$.

subject: Machine learning
title: Q6, cross-entropy loss
stem:
Same model and logits $[3.2, 5.1, 0.8, 2.2, 3.9]$ as the previous question. Compute the
cross-entropy loss, given that the ground truth is class 4. (Multiple answers may be
selected.)
answer:
\textbf{(c) 0.7028, but only with $\log_{10}$.} The loss is
$-\log p_4$ with $p_4 = e^{3.9}/\sum_k e^{z_k} = 0.1982$. With the natural logarithm,
which is what every ML library uses, this is $1.618$, which is not an option; with base
10 it is $0.7029 \approx 0.7028$. (Computed numerically.) So the paper uses $\log_{10}$;
remember that the standard definition uses $\ln$.

subject: Software engineering and web
title: SE Q1, design patterns
stem:
Which design pattern is used to represent an object that encapsulates how a set of
objects interact?
answer:
**(c) Mediator.** This is the Gang of Four definition of Mediator: objects talk to
the mediator instead of to each other, which removes many-to-many coupling (e.g. an air
traffic control tower). Observer (ticked in the screenshot) is a one-to-many
notification scheme, not an object that owns the interaction logic.

subject: Software engineering and web
title: SE Q2, one instance
stem:
Which software design pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides
a global point of access to it?
answer:
**(b) Singleton.** Private constructor plus a static accessor that creates the
instance on first use.

subject: Software engineering and web
title: SE Q3, branch merging
stem: In the context of version control systems (VCS), what does "branch merging" refer to?
options: Creating a new branch from the master branch
Combining changes from one branch into another branch
Deleting a branch after it's no longer needed
Renaming a branch to match a new feature's name
answer:
**(b).** For example `git merge feature` while on `main` brings the
commits of `feature` into `main`.

subject: Software engineering and web
title: SE Q4, SOLID
stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the SOLID principles of object-oriented design?
answer:
**(d) Mutable State Principle**, the intended answer: no such principle exists.
Note that (c) is also misnamed: the "D" of SOLID is the Dependency *Inversion*
Principle. Dependency injection is a technique for applying it, not the principle
itself. The five are SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP.

subject: Software engineering and web
title: SE Q5, cyclomatic complexity
stem: What does the term "cyclomatic complexity" measure in software development?
options: The number of code lines in a program
The number of variables used in a function
The number of linearly independent paths through a program's control flow
The number of classes in an object-oriented system
answer:
**(c).** McCabe's metric $M = E - N + 2P$ on the control-flow graph (edges, nodes,
connected components); for a single function it equals the number of decision points
plus 1.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: DS Q1, open addressing
stem:
Which data structure is commonly used to implement a hash table with open addressing,
where collisions are resolved by searching for the next available slot in the array?
answer:
**(c) Linear probing.** "Searching for the *next* available slot" is linear
probing (try $h, h+1, h+2, \dots$). Quadratic probing tries $h + 1^2, h + 2^2, \dots$;
a linked list is used by separate chaining, the opposite of open addressing. (Strictly,
probing is a collision strategy and the underlying structure is an array.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: DS Q2, AVL balance factor
stem: In the context of data structures, what is the "balancing factor" of an AVL tree?
options: The number of nodes in the left subtree minus the number of nodes in the right subtree
The height of the left subtree minus the height of the right subtree
The number of leaf nodes in the tree
answer:
**(b).** An AVL tree keeps it in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ at every node, rotating when an
insertion or deletion pushes it to $\pm 2$.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: DS Q3, priority queue
stem:
Which data structure is best suited for implementing a priority queue efficiently,
especially with dynamic updates?
answer:
**(c) Binary heap:** $O(\log n)$ insert and extract, $O(1)$ peek, stored compactly in
an array. A balanced BST also gives $O(\log n)$ but with more overhead.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: DS Q4, Dijkstra
stem:
In graph theory, what is the time complexity of finding the shortest path between two
nodes in a weighted graph using Dijkstra's algorithm?
answer:
\textbf{(c) $O(E + V \log V)$}, with a Fibonacci heap. With a binary heap it is
$O((E + V) \log V)$, and with a plain array $O(V^2)$ (best for dense graphs); the
question expects the heap bound.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: DS Q5, simple quadratic sort
stem:
Which sorting algorithm has a worst-case time complexity of $O(n^2)$ but is often used
for its simplicity with small datasets?
answer:
**(c) Bubble sort.** Quicksort is also $O(n^2)$ in the worst case, but it is chosen
for its average-case speed, not its simplicity. (The two screenshots show the candidate
changing the answer from Quick Sort to Bubble Sort.) In practice insertion sort is the
usual choice for small inputs.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: PC Q1, left shift
answer:
**(b) 10.** Inside the parentheses `<<` is the shift operator:
$5 \ll 1 = 101_2 \ll 1 = 1010_2 = 10$. Without the parentheses, `cout << x << 1`
would print `51`.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: PC Q2, inheritance types
stem:
In C++, which type of inheritance allows a class to inherit properties and behaviours
from multiple base classes?
answer:
**(b) Multiple inheritance** (`class C : public A, public B`). Multilevel is a
chain $A \to B \to C$; hierarchical is several classes deriving from one base. The two
screenshots show Hierarchical and then Multilevel ticked; both are wrong.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: PC Q3, const member function
stem:
What does the `const` keyword indicate when used in a C++ (member) function
declaration, as in `int get() const;`?
options: The function does not modify the object it is called on.
answer:
**(c).** Inside a const member function `this` is a pointer to const, so the
data members cannot be changed (except `mutable` ones), and it is the only kind of
member function that can be called on a const object. The screenshot ticks (a).

subject: Python
title: PC Q4, the GIL
stem: In Python, which of the following is true about the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)?
options: GIL allows multiple threads to execute Python code concurrently.
GIL is used to manage memory in Python.
GIL ensures that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.
GIL is a tool for handling exceptions in Python.
answer:
**(c).** So CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel in CPython (use processes);
I/O-bound threads still benefit because the GIL is released while waiting. (Its reason
for existing is to protect the reference counts, but it is a lock, not a memory
manager.)

subject: Python
title: PC Q5, map
stem:
What is the output of the following Python code?

```python
def func(x):
    return x * 2
result = list(map(func, [1, 2, 3, 4]))
print(result)
```
answer:
**(b) `[2, 4, 6, 8]`.** `map` applies `func` to each element;
`[1, 4, 9, 16]` would need `x * x` or `x ** 2`.

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q1, Adam
stem: What is the purpose of the Adam optimizer in deep learning?
options: To perform gradient based parameter updates
answer:
**(d).** Adam is an optimizer: it takes gradients (computed by backpropagation,
not by Adam) and updates the parameters, using running averages of the gradient and of
its square to give each parameter an adaptive step size. It does not regularise
(weight decay is a separate term; AdamW decouples it). The screenshot ticks (b).

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q2, reducing spatial size
stem:
Which layer is used in neural networks for reducing the spatial dimensions of the input
data?
answer:
**(c) Pooling** (e.g. $2 \times 2$ max-pooling halves height and width). A
strided convolution can also downsample, but reducing spatial size is the purpose of
pooling. The screenshot ticks (b).

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q3, activation function
stem: What is the purpose of the activation function in a neural network?
options: To compute the gradient during backpropagation
To introduce non-linearity into the model
answer:
**(c).** Without it, a stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear map.
The screenshot ticks (d).

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q4, fine-tuning
stem: What is fine-tuning in the context of large language models?
options: Adjusting the model's physical hardware for better performance
The process of training the model on specific tasks or datasets
Converting the model's output into different languages
answer:
**(b).** Continue training a pre-trained model (all weights, or a few, as in LoRA)
on task-specific data.

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q5, image classification
stem:
In deep learning, which type of neural network architecture is typically used for image
classification tasks?

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q6, BIC
stem: What is the purpose of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) in model selection?
answer:
**(d) Minimizing overfitting** \unverified. $\mathrm{BIC} = k \ln n - 2 \ln \hat L$
rewards fit (the likelihood term) but penalises the number of parameters $k$, so the
model with the lowest BIC is the one that balances fit against complexity, i.e. the
criterion guards against overfitting. None of the options says "trade-off";
(b) is the next-best reading. It certainly does not minimise bias (the ticked option):
the penalty *increases* bias to reduce variance.

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q7, overfitting
stem: What is the primary challenge of overfitting in machine learning?
answer:
**(b) High variance.** An overfitted model changes a lot with the training sample;
(d) is its symptom. High bias (ticked) is underfitting.

subject: Machine learning
topic: Supervised models (regression, trees, SVM, kNN, Bayes)
title: ML Q8, bagging vs boosting
stem:
What is the difference between bagging and boosting ensemble techniques in machine
learning?
options: Bagging combines multiple weak learners sequentially, while boosting combines them in parallel.
Bagging aims to reduce variance, while boosting aims to reduce bias.
Bagging uses a weighted average of model predictions, while boosting uses a majority vote.
Bagging builds multiple models independently and averages their predictions, while boosting builds models sequentially, giving more weight to misclassified examples.
answer:
**(d)** \unverified. Both (b) and (d) are true statements; (d) describes the
mechanism that defines the two methods and is the usual key for this wording, while (b)
describes the effect. (a) and (c) are reversed.

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q9, vanishing gradients
stem: What is the vanishing gradient problem in deep learning?
options: The weights of the neural network become too large.
Gradients become too small during backpropagation, hindering learning in deep networks.
answer:
**(c).** Backpropagation multiplies many per-layer derivatives; with sigmoid/tanh
these are often below 1 (sigmoid's is at most $0.25$), so the product shrinks
exponentially with depth and the early layers barely learn. Fixes: ReLU, residual
connections, careful initialisation, normalisation, LSTM gates. The screenshot ticks (d).

subject: Machine learning
title: ML Q10, sequence to sequence
stem:
Which deep learning architecture is suitable for sequence-to-sequence tasks like machine
translation?
answer:
**(d) Transformer** \unverified. Encoder-decoder RNNs (including GRU/LSTM
variants) were the original seq2seq models, so (b) and (c) are not wrong, but the
Transformer ("Attention Is All You Need" was introduced *for* machine
translation) is the standard answer today. If only one option can be right, the
question most likely wants the Transformer.

subject: Interview questions
title: rooting a tree as a binary tree, with coloured levels
stem:
You are given an undirected acyclic graph (a tree) in which every vertex has at most 3
neighbours, as an adjacency list.

1. Return a vertex that can be the root of a valid binary tree.
2. *Follow-up.* The vertices are coloured black and white. Return a root of a
    valid binary tree whose levels alternate in colour (B-W-B-W...{} or
    W-B-W-B...), or $-1$ if there is none.
3. *Follow-up.* The vertices are coloured red, black and white. Return a root of
    a valid binary tree whose levels follow the order R-B-W-R-B-W..., starting
    from any of the three colours (B-W-R...{} and W-R-B...{} are allowed, but
    B-R-W is not), or $-1$ if there is none.
answer:
In a tree rooted at $r$, every vertex other than $r$ uses one neighbour as its parent, so
it has at most $3 - 1 = 2$ children. Only the root can have 3 children.

1. Any vertex with at most 2 neighbours is a valid root, and a tree always has a
    leaf, so the answer always exists. $O(n)$.
2. Adjacent vertices are on consecutive levels, so the levels alternate iff
    *every edge joins two different colours*. This does not depend on the root at
    all. If some edge is monochromatic the answer is $-1$; otherwise return any vertex of
    degree $\le 2$.
3. With three colours in cyclic order, a child's colour must be the successor of its
    parent's colour. For an edge $\{u, v\}$ with different colours, exactly one of
    "$v$ follows $u$" and "$u$ follows $v$" holds, so *each edge fixes which end
    is the parent*. An edge with equal colours is impossible. Count the forced parents of
    every vertex. A valid rooting exists iff no vertex has two parents and exactly one
    vertex, the root, has none. Then also check that the root has at most 2 children.
    $O(n)$.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q1, DFS traversal
stem:
Which of the following is/are a valid DFS traversal starting from node 9 of the given
graph? There may be more than one. (Pick one or more.)
[figure: see the original PDF]
(Graph redrawn from the screenshot: edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-4, 4-8, 4-6, 8-7,
7-5, 7-6, 8-9, 9-10, 9-11, 11-12, 11-14, 11-13, 12-14, 12-13.)
answer:
**Only (a).** In a DFS order each new node must be adjacent to the deepest node on
the current path that still has unvisited neighbours.
(b) goes $13 \to 14$, but 13 and 14 are not adjacent and 13 still has the unvisited
neighbour 12. (c) goes $14 \to 13$ while 14's neighbour 12 is unvisited and 13 is not
adjacent to 14. (d) jumps from the $1$-$2$-$3$ triangle back to 4 and then visits 7,
which is not adjacent to 4. (Checked with a program that simulates the DFS stack.)

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q2, male youths who speak German
stem:
30% of the males living in a society know how to speak German. 70% of the males who
know German are adults. The ratio of males to females is $4 : 6$ and the total number
of people is 1000. Calculate the number of males who know German and are not adults.
answer:
**(b) 36.** Males $= 400$; German-speaking males $= 120$; not adults $= 30\%$ of
120 $= 36$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q3, Travel Puzzle 2
stem:
Four couples, the Maceys, Makins, Salmons and Ainsworths, each used a different mode of
transport (car, airplane, bus or ship) to reach their vacation destination, and left
from different cities: Miami, Memphis, Dallas and Washington. Which transport did the
Salmons use?

1. Parker is not married to Paula and did not travel by airplane.
2. David Macey and his wife departed from Miami and did not travel by car.
3. Richard and his wife Rebecca did not travel by bus and did not depart from Memphis.
4. Mike is not married to Ruby Ainsworth. Mike travelled by bus and did not depart from Dallas.
5. Kinsley is not married to Mr. Makin and departed from Washington.
6. The Salmons did not travel by airplane.
7. The couple from Memphis travelled by ship.
answer:
**(a) Bus.** The husbands are David (Macey), Parker, Richard and Mike. Mike
travelled by bus, so Mike is not from Memphis (ship) or Dallas, and not from Miami (the
Maceys): Mike is from Washington, so his wife is Kinsley (clue 5), and they are not the
Makins. Ruby is an Ainsworth and not Mike's wife; Parker is not Paula's husband, so
Parker married Ruby (Ainsworth) and David married Paula. Richard and Rebecca are then
the Makins, so Mike and Kinsley are the Salmons, who travelled by bus. The complete
solution: Macey-Paula, Miami, airplane; Parker-Ruby Ainsworth, Memphis, ship;
Richard-Rebecca Makin, Dallas, car; Mike-Kinsley Salmon, Washington, bus.
(An exhaustive search over all assignments finds exactly this one.)

It is the insertion sort algorithm. Complexity: $O(n^2)$

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q5, TV Ratings 1
stem:
Ten people, A to J, ranked nine TV shows from 1 to 10 as shown below. No two people gave
the same show the same rank. Blank cells are deliberately hidden. What rank did D give
to *Narcos*?
|  | Black Mirror | Making a Murderer | Narcos | Master of None | Mind Hunter | Ozark | Stranger Things | House of Cards | Haunting of Hill House |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2 |  | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 1 |
| B | 4 | 7 | 5 | 9 | 10 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| C | 1 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 6 | 7 |
| D | 6 |  |  | 2 | 7 |  | 4 | 5 | 8 |
| E | 7 | 8 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 4 | 6 | 9 | 3 |
| F | 3 | 5 | 6 | 4 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 1 | 10 |
| G | 5 | 4 | 3 | 6 |  | 9 |  | 7 | 2 |
| H | 10 | 2 |  | 7 | 1 | 3 | 9 | 4 | 5 |
| I | 8 | 1 | 7 | 10 | 3 | 6 | 5 | 2 | 9 |
| J | 9 |  | 10 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 1 | 8 | 4 |
answer:
**(d) 1.** The Narcos column already contains 4, 5, 9, 2, 6, 3, 7, 10, so D and H
hold 1 and 8 between them. H already gave rank 1 (Mind Hunter), and each person uses a
rank once, so H gave Narcos 8 and D gave it 1. (Consistently, D has already used 8,
for Hill House.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q6, process an array
stem:
Given an array of integers `arr` (1-indexed), create a new array `arr'` with
these rules, choosing the data structure that gives optimal performance for large
`arr`. (Every positive integer is a sum of distinct powers of 2.)

1. For each index $i$ that is a power of 2, `arr'[i]` is the sum of
    `arr[1..i]`. E.g. `arr = [2, 3]` gives `arr' = [2, 5]`.
2. For each index $i$ that is even but not a power of 2,
    `arr'[i] = arr[k1] + arr[k2] + ... + arr[km]`, where $k_1, \dots, k_m$ are the
    powers of 2 that sum to $i$. E.g. for $i = 6$, `arr'[6] = arr[2] + arr[4]`.
3. For each odd index $i$, `arr'[i]` is unchanged.

Examples: `[1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1]` $\to$ `[1,2,1,4,1,2,1,8]`;
`[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]` $\to$ `[1,3,3,10,5,6,7,36]`.
options: Create an array and do a prefix sum of all even index elements per the rules.
Implement a binary index tree and update all the even indexes per the rules.
Design a segment tree. For its even indexes, find the powers of 2 that sum to the index and sum the values at those indexes. Save the value to its node.
Create an array. For each even index, iterate the array to determine final values.
answer:
**(a)** \unverified. The output is built once and never queried or updated
afterwards, so a plain array with prefix sums is enough: one $O(n)$ prefix-sum pass
gives every power-of-two entry, and an even index $i$ needs only the original values at
the set bits of $i$ ($O(\log n)$ each), $O(n \log n)$ in total. A Fenwick tree does
*not* store these values (its node 6 holds `arr[5] + arr[6]`, not
`arr[2] + arr[4]`), a segment tree adds overhead with no queries to serve, and (d)
rescans the array for every index ($O(n^2)$). The screenshot shows the cursor on (b),
but no answer is selected.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q7, proportional scores
stem:
A student took four examinations, each worth the same number of points. The marks were
in the proportion $1 : 2 : 3 : 4$. In the first three examinations together, the
student obtained 50% of the total points. On how many exams did the student score more
than 11.11%?
answer:
**(d) 4.** Read "50% of the total points" as 50% of the points available in
those three exams (reading it as 50% of the student's own four-exam total is
impossible, because the first three hold $6/10 = 60\%$ of it). With each exam worth $M$
and marks $k, 2k, 3k, 4k$: $6k = 0.5 \cdot 3M$, so $k = M/4$ and the scores are 25%,
50%, 75%, 100%, all above 11.11%.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q8, Magic Boxes
stem:
There are $n$ boxes with numbers $M[i]$. You start with a ball of size 1; putting it in
box $i$ multiplies its size by $M[i]$, and each box can be used at most once. You win if
the last digit of the ball's size equals $d$. The following scenarios are wins if played
properly; give the maximum possible size of the ball after winning each game.

1. $n = 6$, $d = 4$, $M = \{8, 2, 1, 13, 4, 11\}$
2. $n = 5$, $d = 6$, $M = \{2, 2, 2, 2, 2\}$
3. $n = 6$, $d = 3$, $M = \{9, 4, 8, 11, 5, 17\}$
answer:
**(b) 1144, 16, 1683.**
(1) All boxes give $8 \cdot 2 \cdot 13 \cdot 4 \cdot 11 = 9152$ (ends in 2); dropping 8
gives $1144$ (ends in 4), the largest product ending in 4. (2) $2^k$ ends in 6 only for
$k = 4$ ($2^5 = 32$): 16. (3) Any product with both 4 (or 8) and 5 ends in 0, and 5 with
odd numbers ends in 5, so 5 is out; $9 \cdot 11 \cdot 17 = 1683$ ends in 3 and is the
largest. (All three checked by trying every subset.)

title: Q1, a recursive sequence
stem: A sequence is defined by $a_1 = 2$ and $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$. What is the 4th term?
answer:
**None of the options: the 4th term is 43.** $a_2 = 4 - 2 + 1 = 3$, $a_3 = 9 - 3 + 1
= 7$, $a_4 = 49 - 7 + 1 = 43$ (Sylvester's sequence $2, 3, 7, 43, \dots$). Option (a), 7,
is the *third* term, presumably the intended answer if the setter counted from $a_0$
or misnumbered.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q2, family of six
stem:
In a family of 6 people: A is the father of B; B is the sister of C; D is the mother of E;
E is the son of A; F is the daughter of D. Who is C's mother?
answer:
**(a) D.** B and C are siblings, so both are A's children, and so is E. D is E's
mother, so D is A's wife, and the family's children B, C, E and F are D's children. (Read
strictly, half-siblings would make it "can't be determined", but these puzzles assume
one couple.)

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q3, who is the engineer
stem:
On a train, S, R and J are the fireman, brakeman and engineer, not necessarily in that
order. Also aboard are three businessmen with the same names: Mr. S, Mr. R and Mr. J.

1. Mr. R lives in Dehradun.
2. The brakeman lives exactly halfway between Noida and Dehradun.
3. Mr. J earns exactly Rs. 4,00,000 per year.
4. The brakeman's nearest neighbour, one of the passengers, earns exactly three times
    as much as the brakeman.
5. S beats the fireman in badminton.
6. The passenger whose name is the same as the brakeman's lives in Noida.

Who is the engineer?
answer:
**(b) S.** This is Dudeney's classic puzzle with Indian names.

- The brakeman's neighbour lives halfway between the cities; that is neither
    Mr. R (Dehradun) nor the passenger in Noida. Mr. J's Rs. 4,00,000 is not divisible
    by 3, so the neighbour is not Mr. J either. So the neighbour is Mr. S, and the
    passenger in Noida (clue 6) is Mr. J.
- The brakeman therefore has the same name as Mr. J: J is the brakeman.
- By clue 5, S is not the fireman. So S is the engineer, and R is the fireman.

answer:

In the equation SEND $+$ MORE $=$ MONEY, where each letter is a unique digit 0-9, what is

fifth digit, M, is 1. The full solution is $9567 + 1085 = 10652$, found by brute force.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q8, hens and cows of 729 farmers
stem:
There are 729 farmers in a state, each owning 6 animals, either cows or hens. Last year
there was a flood. The probability of survival of a hen was $1/3$ and that of a cow
$2/3$. How many families have 2 hens and 4 cows?
answer:
**(b) 240**, under the intended (binomial) reading: each of a farmer's 6 surviving
animals is a hen with probability $1/3$ and a cow with probability $2/3$. The expected
number of farmers with exactly 2 hens and 4 cows is

$$729 \binom{6}{2} \left(\tfrac13\right)^2 \left(\tfrac23\right)^4
   = 729 \cdot 15 \cdot \frac{16}{729} = 240.$$

The wording is muddled: survival probabilities alone do not fix how many hens a farmer
owns. The numbers ($729 = 3^6$) only make sense with this reading.

$1 - 1/1.42 = 0.42/1.42 \approx 29.577\%$.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q16, Kuhn's paradigms
stem:
Read the paragraph and answer. Thomas Kuhn's work on scientific paradigms challenged the
view of scientific progress as cumulative. Kuhn proposed episodic revolutions, in which
dominant paradigms are overthrown by anomalies they cannot explain. These revolutions are
not purely rational but involve sociological and psychological factors, as scientists
cling to familiar frameworks until contradictions become unbearable. Paradigm shifts are
then less about absolute truth and more about the prevailing consensus within the
community. Critics say this relativism undermines objectivity; defenders say it captures
the messiness of actual scientific practice. According to the passage, what is the
implication of Kuhn's theory for understanding scientific progress?
options: It validates the notion of universal scientific truth
It emphasizes the linear and rational evolution of science
It confirms the supremacy of modern paradigms over older ones
It suggests that scientific change is contingent and socially influenced
answer:
**(d).** The passage stresses sociological factors and consensus rather than
absolute truth or linear, cumulative progress, which rules out (a), (b) and (c).

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q17, valid GROUP BY / HAVING syntax
stem: Select every expression with correct syntax. (Pick one or more.)
options: `SELECT customer_id, MAX(is_active) FROM transactions GROUP BY customer_id HAVING MAX(is_active)`
`SELECT customer_id, is_active FROM transactions GROUP BY customer_id HAVING MAX(is_active)`
`SELECT customer_id, DISTINCT is_active FROM transactions GROUP BY customer_id HAVING MAX(is_active)`
`SELECT customer_id, MAX(is_active) AS is_active FROM transactions GROUP BY customer_id HAVING is_active`
answer:
**(a) and (d)** (MySQL, which HackerRank uses).

- (a) is fine: `HAVING` may test an aggregate. MySQL treats a non-zero value
    as true.
- (b) selects `is_active` without aggregating or grouping by it. That is
    rejected under the standard rule, which is MySQL's default `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY`
    mode.
- (c) is a syntax error: `DISTINCT` can only follow `SELECT`, not appear
    before a later column.
- (d) is valid in MySQL, which lets `HAVING` refer to a select-list alias.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q18, modelling an expression dependency tree
stem:
What is the best data structure to model the dependency tree used in compilers for parsing
expressions?
answer:
**(c) DAG.** An expression DAG is a syntax tree in which common subexpressions are
shared. Dependencies only point one way, so there are no cycles. A stack is used
*while* parsing, but it does not model the dependencies.

subject: Data structures and algorithms

options: The second key overwrites the first
Both keys are stored in a linked list at that slot
The table size is increased automatically

**(b).** With separate chaining, each slot holds a list (or another container) of
all the entries that hash there. Resizing is a separate load-factor policy, not the
response to a single collision.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q22, triple loop complexity
answer:
\textbf{(c) $O(n^2 \log n)$.} For a given $i$ the middle loop runs about $n/i$ times and
the inner loop $n/2$ times, so the total is
$\sum_i \frac{n}{i} \cdot \frac{n}{2} = \frac{n^2}{2} H_n = \Theta(n^2 \log n)$. Counting
the iterations for $n = 256$ and $1024$ gives a stable ratio to $n^2 \log_2 n$ of about
0.4.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: MAC + MAAR = JOCKO
stem:
What is the sum of 3 times A, 2 times M and 2 times C, if MAC $+$ MAAR $=$ JOCKO (each
letter a different digit)?
answer:
**(b) 31.** A 3-digit plus a 4-digit number with a 5-digit sum forces $J = 1$, and
then $M = 9$ with $O = 0$. The only solution is $932 + 9338 = 10270$ ($M = 9$, $A = 3$, $C
= 2$, $R = 8$, $K = 7$), so $3A + 2M + 2C = 9 + 18 + 4 = 31$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: POINT + ZERO = ENERGY
stem:
If POINT $+$ ZERO $=$ ENERGY (each letter a different digit), then
$E + N + E + R + G + Y = {?}$
answer:
**(a) 17.** A 5-digit plus a 4-digit number with a 6-digit sum forces $E = 1$ and
POINT $\ge 90000$, so $P = 9$. A brute-force search over all assignments finds exactly
one solution, $98504 + 3168 = 101672$, so $E + N + E + R + G + Y = 1 + 0 + 1 + 6 + 7 + 2
= 17$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: TAP + OFF = FILE
stem:
For the cryptarithm TAP $+$ OFF $=$ FILE, assume $T = 8$, $A = 3$ and $P = 5$. What is
the value of LATE?
answer:
**(c) 4386.** A 3-digit plus a 3-digit number with a 4-digit sum forces $F = 1$. Then
the units column $P + F = 5 + 1$ gives $E = 6$, and the tens column $A + F = 3 + 1$ gives
$L = 4$. There are two solutions, $835 + 211 = 1046$ and $835 + 911 = 1746$, but both have
$L = 4$ and $E = 6$, so LATE $= 4386$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: number arrangement machine, step III
stem:
A machine rearranges a line of numbers step by step.
Input: 58 95 37 43 64 42 11 12.
Step I: 14 58 37 43 64 42 12 00.
Step II: 10 14 58 37 43 42 00 01.
Step III: 13 10 14 43 42 00 01 04.
Step IV: 07 13 10 14 00 01 04 02.
Step V: 00 01 02 04 07 10 13 14 (the last step).
For the input 13 56 66 89 99 23 17 33, what is the difference between the highest and the
lowest number in step III?
answer:
**(c) 55.** The rule: in each step the largest remaining input number is replaced
by the sum of its digits, placed at the front, and the smallest by the difference of its
digits, placed at the end. The last step sorts everything. For the new input:

- Step I: 99 $\to$ 18 at the front, 13 $\to$ 02 at the end.
- Step II: 89 $\to$ 17, 17 $\to$ 06.
- Step III: 66 $\to$ 12, 23 $\to$ 01, giving 12 17 18 56 33 02 06 01.

The difference is $56 - 1 = 55$. The rule was checked to reproduce all five example
steps.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: input-output with number blocks
stem:
An input-output is given in steps. Step 1 combines the pairs of 2-digit blocks
$(24, 73)$, $(56, 13)$, $(20, 39)$ into $57$, $49$, $19$; step 2 gives the blocks $25$ and
$58$; step 3 gives $10$ and $40$; step 4 gives $50$. Following the same rules, what is the
final output for the input $54\ 62\ 89\ 25\ 11\ 27$?
answer:
**Not determinable from the photos.** The example fits several rules. Steps 3 and 4
look like "product of the digits" ($2 \cdot 5 = 10$, $5 \cdot 8 = 40$) and "sum"
($10 + 40 = 50$), and step 1 fits "difference of the tens digits, sum of the units
digits". But the arrows of step 2 are not legible, and with the rules that do fit the
example, the new input does not lead to any of the four options. The question is kept for
practice; check the rule with the original test if possible.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: two bus timetables, speed and time
stem:
Bus P runs A (departs 6:00 pm) $\to$ B (arr. 7:30 pm, dep. 7:35 pm, 15 km) $\to$ C
(9:50/10:00 pm, 25 km) $\to$ D (12:00/12:10 am, 60 km) $\to$ E (2:30/2:45 am, 100 km)
$\to$ F (arrives 4:00 am, 200 km). Bus Q runs F (7:00 pm) $\to$ E (8:40/8:45 pm, 10 km)
$\to$ D (10:30/10:35 pm, 25 km) $\to$ C (11:40/11:45 am, 65 km) $\to$ B (4:00/4:10 am,
200 km) $\to$ A (arrives 7:00 am, 300 km). The column with the distances is headed
"distance from origin".

1. Find the difference between the speeds of bus P and bus Q (in km/h). Options:
    11, 10, 12, 8.
2. If bus P increases its average speed by 25%, find the time it reaches its
    destination. Options: 1:45 am, 2:00 am, 2:45 am, 1:00 am.
answer:
1. **10.** Read literally (distances from the origin), P covers 200 km in 10 h
    (20 km/h) and Q 300 km in 12 h (25 km/h), a difference of 5, which is not an option.
    The keyed answer 10 comes from *adding* the column, as if each entry were the
    distance from the previous station: P covers 400 km in 10 h (40 km/h) and Q 600 km in
    12 h (50 km/h). So the setter's table really gives station-to-station distances.
2. **2:00 am.** A 25% higher average speed cuts the 10-hour journey to
    $10 / 1.25 = 8$ hours, whichever reading of the distances is used, so the bus arrives
    at $6\text{ pm} + 8\text{ h} = 2{:}00$ am.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: two bus timetables, income ratio
stem:
With the timetables of the previous question, and also the number of people boarding and
the fare per person at each station (bus P: 25, 30, 20, 10, 30 boarding at A-E, fares
$-, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300$ at A-F; bus Q: 30, 10, 20, 25, 15 boarding at F-B, fares
$-, 20, 40, 50, 90, 200$ at F-A): the total income of bus P is what percentage of the
total income of bus Q?
answer:
**Ambiguous; none of the natural readings gives an option exactly.**

- Passengers boarding at a station pay that station's fare: $11000 / 3600 =
    305.6\%$.
- Everyone rides to the terminus and pays (final fare $-$ boarding fare):
    $23500 / 16400 = 143.3\%$.
- Passengers pay the fare listed at the next station: $251.7\%$, closest to (d)
    250%.

The table does not say where passengers get off, which is what the income depends on.
In an exam, choose (d), the option nearest to the only reading that comes close; but treat
the question as flawed.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: ten cars in two facing rows
stem:
Ten cars (red, black, green, white, yellow, pink, blue, grey, violet, orange), numbered 1
to 10, are parked in two rows of five facing each other; each car is exactly opposite one
car of the other row. No odd-numbered car is opposite another odd-numbered car, and no two
even-numbered cars are adjacent. Left and right are as seen by each driver.

1. The pink car is numbered 8 and is not in the same row as cars 4 and 6.
2. White and yellow are adjacent to car 6, but white is not at an end.
3. Blue is numbered 5 and is not in the same row as cars 3 and 6.
4. Red is neither adjacent nor opposite to blue or green.
5. Pink is at the right end of its row.
6. Car 6 is second from the right in its row.
7. Black is even-numbered and opposite car 1.
8. Violet and orange are in the same row; car 6 is not to the left of car 7.
9. Green is odd-numbered but not 1, and in the same row as blue.
10. Yellow is opposite car 2 and numbered neither 3 nor 1.

**Q1.** Which numbers are parked in the same row? Options: 1, 3, 4, 6, 9 /
2, 3, 8, 9, 10 / 5, 7, 8, 2, 9 / 4, 1, 9, 7, 10.
**Q2.** If the green car is adjacent to the grey car, which car is opposite car 4?
Options: 7, 5, cannot be determined, 1.
answer:
**Q1: 1, 3, 4, 6, 9. Q2: 5.** A program tried every assignment of numbers and colours
under all ten clues. Every surviving arrangement has the rows $\{1, 3, 4, 6, 9\}$ and
$\{2, 5, 7, 8, 10\}$; eight arrangements survive, differing only in details the questions
do not ask about.

By hand: one odd per column and no adjacent evens force one row to have evens in columns
1, 3, 5 and the other in 2, 4. Pink 8 is at a right end, and car 6 is second from the
right in the *other* row (clue i), so 6 and 8 are in different rows; blue 5 is with
8 (clue iii), and 4 is with 6 (clue i). Black is opposite 1, yellow opposite 2, green is
odd and with 5, and so on.

In every arrangement where green is next to grey, car 5 is opposite car 4.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: doors, roads, fruit and flowers
stem:
Statements: All doors are roads. No road is fruit. Some flowers are doors.
Conclusions: I. Some fruits are doors. II. Some fruits are flowers. III. Some roads are
flowers. IV. No fruit is a flower.
options: Only either II or IV follows
Only either II or III, and IV follow
Only either II or IV, and I follow
Only either II or IV, and III follow
answer:
**(d) Only either II or IV, and III follow.**

- III follows: some flowers are doors, and all doors are roads.
- I is false: doors are roads and no road is fruit, so no door is a fruit.
- II and IV are not definite, but they are a complementary pair ("some ... are"
    and "no ... is" about the same two sets), so exactly one of them holds.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: coding PARTY with two letter matrices
stem:
Each letter is coded by its row number then its column number in one of two matrices.
Matrix 1 (rows and columns 0-4), row by row: P R Y F Q / Q F R Y P / R Q P Y F /
F P Q R Y / Y Q P F R. Matrix 2 (rows and columns 5-9): T Z A G W / Z A G W T /
W T A G Z / A G W T Z / G T Z W A. Which set of numbers can represent the word PARTY?
answer:
**(d).** Check each code: P $= 00$ (row 0, column 0), A $= 66$, R $= 44$, T $= 88$,
Y $= 23$. Every other option fails at its first or second code: for example, $40$ is Y,
$12$ is R, and in (c) $31$ is P, not A.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: only mathematics, from a Venn diagram
stem:
A Venn diagram of 100 students shows mathematics only $= x$, both subjects $= 28$, physics
only $= x(x - 10)$, and neither $= 36$. Find the probability that a randomly chosen student
studies only mathematics.
answer:
\textbf{(d) $12/100$.} $x + 28 + x(x - 10) + 36 = 100$ gives $x^2 - 9x - 36 = 0$, so
$x = 12$ (the other root, $-3$, is impossible).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: three languages in a town of 400
stem:
In a town of 400 people, 185 speak Latin, 165 speak German and 160 speak French. 40 people
speak only French and Latin, 20 speak only German and Latin, and 10 speak only French and
German. How many people speak only one language?
answer:
**(b) 310**, assuming everyone speaks at least one of the three. Let $t$ people speak
all three. The single-language speakers number $185 + 165 + 160 - 2 \cdot 70 - 3t =
370 - 3t$, and the whole town is $(370 - 3t) + 70 + t = 440 - 2t = 400$, so $t = 20$ and
the answer is $370 - 60 = 310$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: who robbed the bank
stem:
Tom, Martin and Garry are suspects in a bank robbery; only one of them is guilty. Tom
says he is innocent. Martin says he is innocent. Garry says Martin is the guilty one. Who
robbed the bank, if only one statement is true?
answer:
**(a) Tom.** If Tom is guilty, only Martin's statement is true. If Martin is guilty,
Tom and Garry both tell the truth; if Garry is guilty, Tom and Martin both do.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: figure rotated 135 degrees then back 45
stem:
Choose the figure that, after being rotated $135^\circ$ clockwise and then $45^\circ$
counter-clockwise, is identical to the question figure. (The figure and the four options
are drawings and are not reproduced.)
answer:
The two rotations add up to $90^\circ$ clockwise. So the required option is the question
figure turned $90^\circ$ *counter-clockwise*: rotating that option $90^\circ$
clockwise gives back the question figure. Check one asymmetric detail of the figure
(here, the side the small attachment points to) rather than the whole shape.

subject: Interview questions
title: situational judgement, heated argument
stem:
You are in a heated argument with a friend and both of you are becoming disrespectful and
insulting. What is the best reaction?
options: Confront the friend about their behaviour.
Agree to disagree and end the argument.
Continue the argument and insult the friend back.
answer:
**(c) Agree to disagree and end the argument** is the response these tests
usually reward. It de-escalates without abandoning the relationship. Walking away (a) is
the second-best choice; (b) and (d) escalate.

subject: Interview questions
title: situational judgement, two job offers
stem:
You have been offered two jobs: one with a higher salary but longer working hours, and one
with a lower salary but shorter working hours. What do you do?
options: Choose the job with the higher salary.
Choose the job with the shorter working hours.
Negotiate shorter working hours with the job with a higher salary.
Negotiate a higher salary with the job with shorter working hours.
answer:
There is no objectively correct option; the question tests judgement. Situational tests
usually reward the proactive, balanced choices (c) or (d), which try to get the best of
both offers instead of accepting a trade-off without trying. In an interview, explain the
reasoning: what matters more to you at this stage, and why.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q4
stem: Choose the option that conforms most closely to Standard English usage.
options: We are forced to fall back on fatalism as an explanation of irrational events.
We are forced to falling back on the fatalism as an explanation of irrational events.
We are forced to fall back to fatalism as an explanation of irrational events.
We are forced to fall back on fatalism as explanations of irrational events.
answer:
**(a).** The idiom is "fall back *on*"; "forced to" takes the bare
infinitive (not "falling"); fatalism is *an* explanation (singular), and
"the fatalism" adds a needless article.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q9
stem: Choose the option that conforms most closely to Standard English usage.
options: The running of a large business consists of getting somebody to sell something that somebody else made for more than it cost.
The running of large businesses consist of getting somebody to make something that somebody else sold to somebody else for more than its cost.
The running of large businesses consist of getting somebody to make something else that somebody else will sell to somebody else for more than it costs.
The running of a large business consists of getting somebody to make something that somebody else will sell to somebody else for more than it costs.
answer:
**(e).** The subject is "the running", which is singular, so the verb must be
"consists"; that rules out (b) and (c). (a) changes the meaning ("sell something
that somebody else made") and mixes tenses. (e) is grammatical and keeps the
tenses consistent ("will sell ... costs"). The photo ticks (c), which has the
agreement error.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q10, sentence correction
stem:
NASA reports that ancient observers took note of solar eclipses at least as far back
as 2500 BC, *as evidenced by surviving records from* ancient Babylon and China.
options: as evidenced by records that have survived in
as the evidence that has survived from the records of
as shows the evidence of records surviving in
as the surviving records show the evidence of
answer:
**(b) No correction required.** "As evidenced by" correctly introduces the
evidence for the whole claim, and "surviving records from" is concise. (a) says
the records survived *in* Babylon, which changes the meaning; (c)-(e) are
ungrammatical or wordy.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q11, sentence correction
stem: *It was until many years* later that Gandhi became a rebel against authority.
options: It was not until many years
answer: **(a).** The idiom is "It was *not until* ... that ...".

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q14, spot the error
stem:
Choose the option which contains a mistake. (The parts form the sentence
"This has slowed the progress / of reforms in many countries / because the choice of
either of the extreme / positions inevitably invite criticism.")
options: because the choice of either of the extreme
answer:
**(c).** The subject of "invite" is "the choice" (singular), so it must be
"invites".

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q15, sentence correction
stem: The farmer *was fool apparently* to believe him.
answer:
**(b) was apparently a fool.** "Fool" is a countable noun and needs "a";
the adverb sits naturally between the verb and its complement.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q22, sentence correction
stem: There is no doubt *whether he will be* punished for his wrong doings.
answer:
**(a) that he will be.** "No doubt" is followed by "that"; "doubt
whether" is used only when there *is* doubt.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q1, breaking a chocolate bar
stem:
Santa and Banta play a game with a chocolate bar 15 squares long and 20 squares wide.
Santa begins by breaking the bar in two along any division. Banta then picks up any
piece and breaks it in two, and so on. Who will be the first player who cannot make
any more moves?
answer:
**(c) Banta.** Every break increases the number of pieces by exactly one, so
going from 1 piece to $15 \cdot 20 = 300$ single squares takes exactly 299 breaks,
however they are made. Santa makes the odd-numbered breaks, including the 299th, so
Banta is the first who cannot move.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q8, black and white balls
stem:
A bag contains 25 white balls and 50 black ones; a separate pile of black balls is
also available. The following two-step operation is repeated. First, two balls are
drawn at random from the bag. Then:

- if both are black, one is put back in the bag and the other thrown away;
- if one is black and the other white, the white one is put back and the black
    one thrown away;
- if both are white, both are thrown away and a black ball from the pile is put
    into the bag.

The bag loses a ball at each step, so eventually it holds a single ball. What colour
is it?
options: Cannot be determined, but most likely Black
Cannot be determined, but most likely White
answer:
**(c) White.** The number of white balls changes by 0 (first two cases) or
by $-2$ (third case), so its parity never changes. It starts at 25, which is odd, so
it can never reach 0: the last ball is white. (The candidate left this one blank.)

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q12, spokes
stem:
A bicycle shop has some unique bicycles. Each bike is identical, and each bike's
front and back wheels have at least one spoke each. You don't know how many bicycles
are in the shop, but you know there are between 200 and 300 spokes in total.
If you knew the exact number of spokes, you would be able to figure out the number of
bicycles. You don't know the exact number of spokes, but just knowing the fact that
you would be able to figure it out with that information lets you deduce the answer.
How many bicycles and spokes are there?
answer:
**(a) 17 bicycles with 17 spokes each (289 spokes).** With $b \ge 2$ bicycles
of $s \ge 2$ spokes each (two wheels, at least one spoke per wheel), the total is
$S = bs$. The number of bicycles is determined by $S$ only if $S$ has exactly one
factorisation $b \cdot s$ with $b, s \ge 2$, which happens exactly when $S = p^2$ for
a prime $p$. The only such number between 200 and 300 is $289 = 17^2$. (Checked by
listing the factorisations of 200-300.) The last option is a stray option copied
from another question.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q17, symbol pattern
answer:
**(b) 143542.** For $a+b+c$ the result is $ab$, then $ac$, then the digits of
$(a+c)\cdot b$ reversed: $5+2+2 \to 10, 10, 14 \to 41$;
$9+2+4 \to 18, 36, 26 \to 62$; $8+6+3 \to 48, 24, 66$; $5+4+5 \to 20, 25, 40 \to 04$.
So $7+2+5 \to 14, 35, 24 \to 42$, giving 143542. The photo ticks 143554, from the
wrong last block $(9)\times 5$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q18, floor puzzle
stem:
Eight persons live on eight different floors of a building; the ground floor is
numbered 1 and the top floor 8. Y lives on an even-numbered floor. Two persons live
between Y and K. T lives on one of the floors above H, and both live on even-numbered
floors. O lives just above L. Two persons live between Y and X. M does not live above
Y. X lives on one of the floors below K. Who lives on the topmost floor?
answer:
**(b) T.** The only arrangement (bottom to top) is
X, H, M, Y, L, O, K, T. Y must be on floor 4: K and X are both 3 floors from Y with
X below K, so X $=$ Y$-3$ and K $=$ Y$+3$. Then T and H take the even floors 2 and 8
with T above H, M goes on floor 3 (below Y), and L, O fill 5, 6. (An exhaustive search
over all $8!$ arrangements finds exactly this one.) The photo ticks K, from a working
that puts T on floor 7, which is odd.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q19, number sequence
stem: Find the next term in the sequence: 2, 18, 52, 110, ...
answer:
**(d) 198.** The differences are 16, 34, 58 and their differences 18, 24, so the
next second difference is 30, the next difference 88, and the next term
$110 + 88 = 198$. Equivalently the terms are $n^3 + 3n^2 - 2$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q21, same place same time
stem:
You start at 8 am from Delhi and drive towards Jaipur (at variable speed, taking random
breaks), reaching Jaipur at 12 noon. The next day you start at 8 am from Jaipur, take
the same road back and reach Delhi at 12 noon (again at variable speed, with random
breaks). How likely is it that there is a point on the road which you crossed at the
same time of day on both journeys?
answer:
**(c) 100%.** Imagine both journeys on the same day: one car goes from Delhi to
Jaipur and the other from Jaipur to Delhi between 8 am and noon. They must meet, and
at that moment they are at the same point at the same time (intermediate value
theorem applied to the difference of the two positions).

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q23, fastest horses
stem:
You have 25 horses and want the fastest 3. In each race only 5 horses can run at the
same time. What is the minimum number of races needed to find the three fastest
horses without using a stopwatch?
answer:
**(a) 7.** Five heats (5 races), then a race of the five winners (6th) gives the
fastest horse. The candidates for 2nd and 3rd are only: the 2nd and 3rd of the
winners' race, the 2nd and 3rd of the fastest horse's heat, and the 2nd of the
heat of the horse that came 2nd in the winners' race. Racing these five (7th race)
settles it.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q2, four missiles
stem:
Four missiles start from the four corners of a 2 m square, each homing on to (aiming
at) the missile on its left. The missiles fly at 1 m/s. How long would it take them to
meet? (Ignore gravity.)
answer:
**(a) 2 s.** By symmetry the missiles always form a shrinking square. Each
missile moves straight at its target, and the target's velocity is perpendicular to
that line, so the distance between them shrinks at the full speed 1 m/s. They meet
when the initial separation, the side of 2 m, is used up: $2/1 = 2$ s.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q3, cost of running a train
stem:
The rate of coal consumption of a locomotive varies as the square of its speed and is
1000 kg per hour at 60 km/h. If coal costs Rs 15 per 100 kg and the other expenses
of the train are Rs 12 per hour, find a formula for the cost in paise per kilometre
when the speed is $X$ km/h.
answer:
\textbf{(a) $1200/X + 75X/18$.} Coal per hour is $1000 X^2/3600$ kg at 15 paise per
kg, i.e. $15000X^2/3600 = 25X^2/6$ paise per hour; other costs are 1200 paise per
hour. The train covers $X$ km in an hour, so the cost per km is
$1200/X + 25X/6 = 1200/X + 75X/18$. (Check at $X = 60$: $20 + 250 = 270$ paise.)
The photo ticks (c), which is a cost per *hour* with the wrong constant.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q5, flashing light
stem:
If a light flashes every 6 seconds, how many times will it flash in $\tfrac34$ of an
hour?
answer:
**(c) 451** is the standard answer. $\tfrac34$ hour $= 2700$ s gives
$2700/6 = 450$ intervals, and counting the flash at the very start there are
$450 + 1 = 451$ flashes. The photo ticks 450, which counts intervals rather than
flashes. \unverified{} (the question does not say whether the first flash is at time 0,
but 451 is the usual key for this question).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q6, partnership
stem:
A, B and C start a business. A invests Rs 6500 for 6 months, B Rs 8400 for 5 months
and C Rs 10{,}000 for 3 months. A is the working member and receives 5% of the
profits for it. The profit earned is Rs 7400. Calculate B's share of the profit.
answer:
**(a) Rs 2660.** A first takes $5\% \cdot 7400 = 370$, leaving 7030 to be shared in
the ratio of capital $\times$ time: $39000 : 42000 : 30000 = 39 : 42 : 30$. B gets
$7030 \cdot 42/111 = 2660$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q7, sets
stem:
Last year 26 members of a club travelled to England, 26 to France and 32 to Italy.
No member travelled to both England and France, 6 travelled to both England and
Italy, and 11 travelled to both France and Italy. How many members travelled to at
least one of these three countries?
answer:
**(a) 67.** Since nobody visited both England and France, nobody visited all
three. Inclusion-exclusion: $26 + 26 + 32 - 0 - 6 - 11 + 0 = 67$. (Regions:
England only 20, France only 15, Italy only 15, England-Italy 6, France-Italy 11.)
The photo ticks 52, from a Venn diagram with wrong region counts.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q13, work and wages
stem:
A alone can do a piece of work in 6 days and B alone in 8 days. A and B undertook to
do it for Rs 3200. With the help of C, they completed the work in 3 days. How much is
to be paid to C?
answer:
**(a) Rs 400.** In 3 days A does $\tfrac36$ and B $\tfrac38$ of the work, together
$\tfrac{7}{8}$; C did the remaining $\tfrac18$ and is paid $\tfrac18 \cdot 3200 = 400$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q16, lock codes
stem:
A three-digit code for certain locks uses the digits 0-9 under these constraints: the
first digit cannot be 0 or 1, the second digit must be 0 or 1, and the second and
third digits cannot both be 0. How many different codes are possible?
answer:
**(d) 152.** First digit: 8 choices; second: 2; third: 10, giving 160; subtract
the $8$ codes with second and third digits both 0: $160 - 8 = 152$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q20, digit reversal
stem:
How many two-digit numbers are there which, when added to the number formed by
interchanging their digits, give a perfect square?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q24, mixing tea
stem:
In what ratio should a shopkeeper mix tea costing Rs 120 per kg and Rs 180 per kg so
that by selling the mixture at Rs 205 per kg he earns a profit of 25%?
answer:
**(b) 4 : 11.** The cost price of the mixture is $205/1.25 = 164$. By
alligation the ratio is $(180 - 164) : (164 - 120) = 16 : 44 = 4 : 11$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q25, snowfall and a liar
stem:
A father claims there was snowfall last night. The first daughter says that the
probability of snowfall on a particular night is $1/8$. The second daughter says that
the father lies 5 times out of 6. What is the probability that there actually was a
snowfall?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q10, the person in the photograph
stem:
Pointing to a person in a photograph, Anjali said, "He is the only son of the father of my
sister's brother." How is that person related to Anjali?
answer:
**(d) None of these.** The father of her sister's brother is her own father, and his
only son is her brother.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q11, measuring 45 minutes with two ropes
stem:
You have two ropes, each taking exactly 60 minutes to burn, but they burn unevenly. How can
you measure 45 minutes?
options: Burn one rope halfway then the other fully.
Burn one rope from both ends and the other from one end.
Burn both ropes from one end.
Burn both ropes from both ends.
answer:
**(b).** The rope lit at both ends burns out after 30 minutes. At that moment, light
the other end of the second rope; its remaining 30 minutes of burn now take 15, giving 45.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q12, seven students on three benches
stem:
Seven students A to G sit on benches I, II and III, at least two per bench and at least one
girl per bench. C, a girl, does not sit with A, E or D. F, a boy, sits with only B. A sits
on bench I with his best friends. G sits on bench III. E is the brother of C. Which group
consists of girls?
answer:
**(a) BCD.** F sits with only B, so $\{F, B\}$ is a bench, and B is its girl. C cannot
sit with A, D or E, so she sits with G on bench III, and bench I is $\{A, D, E\}$. A
("his") and E ("brother") are boys, so D is that bench's girl.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q13, length of a fish
stem:
A fish's head is 10 cm long; its tail is the length of the head plus one third of the
length of the body; the body equals the head plus twice the tail. What is the fish's total
length?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q14, clock hands in a straight line
stem: At what time between 11 and 12 o'clock will the hands of a clock form a straight line?
answer:
**(a) about 27 minutes past 11.** At $t$ minutes past 11 the hands are at
$330 + 0.5t$ and $6t$ degrees; opposite means $330 + 0.5t - 6t = 180$, so
$t = 300/11 = 27\tfrac{3}{11}$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q14 (other set), approximate the value
stem: Find the value of $49 / 212 \times 199 - 206 + 195$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q16, men catching sharks
stem:
40 men can catch 200 sharks in 20 days working 6 hours a day. In how many days can 25 men
catch 300 sharks working 4 hours a day?
answer:
**72 days; none of the options.** One shark takes $40 \cdot 20 \cdot 6 / 200 = 24$
man-hours, so 300 sharks take 7200, and $25 \times 4 = 100$ man-hours a day gives 72 days.
The numbers as photographed do not produce any listed option.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q17, letter series R T P R N P
stem: Which is the next letter in the series R, T, P, R, N, P?
answer:
**(b) L.** Two interleaved series, each going back two letters: R, P, N, L and
T, R, P.

subject: Verbal ability
title: Q18, conclusion of the billiards argument
stem:
"People say that playing billiards is the best way to burn calories, but this is not true.
Since playing billiards requires very little physical effort, billiards does not help in
burning many calories." What is the main conclusion?
options: People say that playing billiards is the best way to burn calories.
Playing billiards is not the best way to burn calories.
Playing billiards does not burn many calories.
Playing billiards requires little physical exertion.
answer:
**(b).** The argument exists to reject the popular claim; (d) is the premise and (c)
the intermediate step supporting it.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: largest common divisor of three numbers
stem: What is the largest integer that divides 23400, 272304 and 205248 without remainder?
answer:
**(c) 24** $= \gcd(23400, 272304, 205248)$. For example, $23400 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2
\cdot 5^2 \cdot 13$ has only three factors of 2, which already rules out 48 and 96.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: next pair in 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 4, 8
stem: Choose the next pair in the series 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 4, 8.
answer:
**Ambiguous.** The odd positions run $2, 4, 6, 8$, so 10 is next at position 9, but the
even positions $3, 5, 4$ follow no clear rule. Reading the pairs as $(2,3), (4,5), (6,4)$,
the next pair starts with 8, which no option does. Option (d) $9, 10$ is the only one
consistent with the odd-position series; treat the question as unverified.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q23, all-pairs shortest paths with negative edges
stem:
Which algorithm determines the shortest path between all pairs of vertices in a graph whose
edges may have positive or negative weights, with no negative cycles?
answer:
**(d) Floyd-Warshall**, $O(V^3)$. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges but from a
single source; Dijkstra needs non-negative weights; Kruskal builds spanning trees.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q27, virtual destructor output
stem: What is the output of the following C++ code?
answer:
**(a) 134212.** `new B` runs the constructors base-first (1, 3). `~A` is
virtual, so deleting through `A*` runs `~B` then `~A` (4, 2). `new A`
and its deletion print 1 and 2. Compiled and run: `134212`. Without `virtual`,
the first delete would print only 2 (and be undefined behaviour).

subject: Computer networks
title: Q28, subnet mask for 70 subnets of 480 hosts
stem:
Which subnet mask should you use for the network 172.29.0.0 to get 70 subnets with 480 hosts
per subnet?
answer:
**(d) 255.255.254.0** (/23). This class B network has 16 host bits. 70 subnets need 7
subnet bits ($2^7 = 128$), leaving 9 host bits: $2^9 - 2 = 510 \ge 480$.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q29, assignment inside if
stem: What is the output of the following C++ code?
answer:
**(a) world.** `if (i = 5)` *assigns* 5, and the condition is non-zero, so
the first iteration prints `world` and breaks. GCC warns "suggest parentheses around
assignment used as truth value". Compiled and run.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q30, edges of a spanning tree
stem: A graph has 10 vertices and 15 edges. How many edges does a minimum spanning tree have?
answer:
**(b) 9**: a spanning tree on $V$ vertices has $V - 1$ edges, whatever $E$ is
(assuming the graph is connected).

subject: Operating systems
title: Q31, reducing context-switch time
stem:
In an operating system, which of the following reduces the context-switch time?
(1) Minimise the amount of memory of a process to be swapped. (2) Increase the speed of the
disk used for swapped-out processes. (3) Overlap swapping and program execution.
(4) Maximise the amount of memory of a process to be swapped.
answer:
**(b) 1, 2 and 3.** When a switch involves swapping, its cost is dominated by the
transfer: less memory to move (1), a faster disk (2) and overlapping the transfer with
execution (3) all cut it; (4) makes it worse. (Some keys give (a), counting only the OS
design choices and treating faster hardware as outside the question.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q32, statements about BFS and DFS
stem:
Which statements are correct? (1) BFS and DFS are algorithms for traversing and searching a
node in a graph. (2) BFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.
(3) DFS uses a strategy opposite to BFS: it explores the deepest node first before being
forced to backtrack and expand other nodes.
answer:
**(e) None.** Statements 1 and 3 are correct and 2 is false (it describes DFS); no
option says "1 and 3".

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q33, sailors who reserved a red boat
answer:
**(b).** Both join conditions are needed. Without `R.bid = B.bid`, any sailor
with any reservation qualifies whenever some red boat exists; without
`S.sid = R.sid`, every sailor qualifies.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q34, counting distinct addresses
stem:
STUDENT has addresses Chicago, New York, Boston, Seattle, Chicago, New York. What does
`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ADDRESS FROM STUDENT);` return?
answer:
**(a) 4** distinct addresses. A caveat worth mentioning in an interview: MySQL and
SQL Server reject a derived table without an alias ("Every derived table must have its
own alias"), so there the query is an error; SQLite, PostgreSQL 16+ and Oracle accept it.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q35, not a WHERE-clause operator
stem: In SQL, which of the following is not an operator for the WHERE clause?
answer: **(b) IN BETWEEN.** `IN` and `BETWEEN` are separate operators.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q36, rows of a cross join
stem:
Students has 100 rows and Course has 5. How many rows does
`SELECT * FROM Students, Course;` return?
answer:
**(a) 500**: listing tables without a join condition is a Cartesian product,
$100 \times 5$.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q36 (other set), EXISTS with ORDER BY
stem:
CUSTOMER(CUSTID, NAME): 4000 Mike, 5000 Tara, 6000 Alice, 7000 Bob, 8000 Mary, 9000 John.
ORDER has orders by customers 7000, 5000, 8000 and 4000. What does
`SELECT NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM ORDER WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTID = ORDER.CUSTID) ORDER BY NAME;`
return?
answer:
**(a) Bob Mary Mike Tara**: the customers with at least one order, sorted by name.
Strictly, `ORDER` is a reserved word and the table would need quoting in real SQL,
which makes "Error" tempting; the test intends the logical result.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: Q1, I2C
stem: I2C is a:
answer:
**(d) Multi-master, multi-slave.** Every device has an address and any master can
start a transfer; arbitration on SDA resolves collisions.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q2, cache hits
stem: What determines the high hit rate of cache memory? (more than one answer possible)
answer:
**(b) Size of cache**; a larger cache holds more of the working set. (Mapping and
replacement policy matter too.) Adding cache levels can raise the combined hit rate, so
(c) is defensible \unverified. RAM size and access speed do not change the hit rate;
speed changes hit *time*.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
topic: Instruction set, addressing modes and CPU design
title: Q3, accumulator
stem: What is the purpose of the accumulator?
options: Storing data and performing logical operations
Storing data and performing arithmetic operations
answer:
**(c)** \unverified. The accumulator is the register that holds one operand and the
result of every ALU (arithmetic *and* logical) operation; the ALU does the work, so
(c) is the intended reading. (a) and (b) each name only one kind of operation, and (d)
describes address registers.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: Q4, ARM Abort mode
stem: During what scenarios is Abort mode entered? (more than one answer possible)
options: An attempt to access memory fails
The processor is in rest state
answer:
**(b).** ARM enters Abort mode on a prefetch or data abort, that is when a memory
access fails. Undefined instructions use Undefined mode.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: Q5, interrupts
stem: An interrupt diverts the execution of the processor to:
answer: **(a) The interrupt service routine.**

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: Q6, ignorable interrupt
stem: An interrupt that can be temporarily ignored is a:
answer: **(c) Maskable interrupt.**

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q7, memory interleaving
stem: In memory interleaving, the lower-order bits of the address are used to:
options: get the address of the module
get the address of the data within the module
answer:
**(b) Select the module.** In low-order interleaving consecutive words go to
consecutive modules, so the low bits pick the module and the high bits the word inside it.

subject: Operating systems
title: Q8, terminating signals
stem: Which signals are best suited to terminate a process? (more than one answer)
answer:
**(a) and (b).** SIGTERM asks politely (can be handled) and SIGKILL cannot be caught.
SIGSEGV reports a memory fault and SIGINT is the terminal's Ctrl-C interrupt; both end the
process by default but are not the tools for terminating one.

subject: C programming
title: Q9, the malloc free list
stem:
Which is true? (1) When `malloc` allocates a block it allocates extra bytes to hold an
integer containing the size of the block. (2) The list of free blocks is a doubly linked
list.
answer:
**(c) Only 1** \unverified. Allocators keep a header with the block size (that is how
`free` knows the size). The classic K&R allocator keeps a singly linked circular free
list; real allocators vary, so (2) is not true in general.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q10, cache writing
stem:
(Only the heading was photographed.) Which cache write policy is used when the cache is
updated but main memory is not updated? [cut off in the source]
answer:
**Write-back**: memory is updated only when the dirty line is evicted. (Write-through
updates both at once.)

subject: Operating systems
title: Q11, system()
stem: How many times is `fork` called inside `system()`?
answer:
**(a) Once.** `system()` forks one child, which `exec`s `/bin/sh -c`
with the command, and waits for it.

subject: Operating systems
title: Q12, zombies
stem:
Which are true of zombie processes? (1) They are killed by SIGKILL. (2) They are removed
by `wait()`. (3) One is created when a child terminates before its parent waits for it.
answer:
**(b) 2 and 3.** A zombie is already dead, so no signal can kill it; only the parent's
`wait` (or the parent's death, making `init` reap it) removes it.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: Q13, filtered white noise
stem:
Zero-mean white Gaussian noise is passed through an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth
10 kHz and the output is sampled every $T_s = 0.03$ ms. The samples are:
answer:
**(a) Correlated.** The output autocorrelation is $R(\tau) \propto
\operatorname{sinc}(2B\tau)$, which is zero only at $\tau = k/(2B) = 0.05k$ ms. 0.03 ms is
not such a lag, so neighbouring samples are correlated. (At $T_s = 0.05$ ms they would be
uncorrelated and, being Gaussian, independent.)

subject: Operating systems
topic: System calls, kernel and general OS
title: Q14, character devices
stem: Which of the following is a character device?
answer:
**(d) Terminals.** They transfer a stream of characters with no seeking. Disks and
disk-on-key drives are block devices. (A webcam is also exposed as a character device on
Linux, but the textbook answer is the terminal.)

subject: Mathematics
title: Q15, integral over the real line
stem: An integral from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ is:
answer:
**(a) Definite** (an improper definite integral: it has limits and evaluates to a
number when it converges).

subject: Mathematics
title: Q16, perpendicular unit vector
stem:
A unit vector perpendicular to both $\mathbf a = \mathbf i + 2\mathbf j + \mathbf k$ and
$\mathbf b = \mathbf j + 2\mathbf k$ is:
answer:
**(b).** $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = (2 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1)\mathbf i - (1 \cdot 2 -
1 \cdot 0)\mathbf j + (1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 0)\mathbf k = 3\mathbf i - 2\mathbf j + \mathbf k$,
of length $\sqrt{14}$.

subject: Mathematics
title: Q17, a linear ODE
stem: The general solution of $\dfrac{dx}{dt} + 2x = 6$ is:
answer:
\textbf{(d) $Ce^{-2t} + 3$}: homogeneous part $Ce^{-2t}$ plus the constant particular
solution $x = 6/2 = 3$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q19, more heads than tails
stem: A fair coin is flipped 7 times. What is the probability of getting more heads than tails?
answer:
**(d) 32/64 = 1/2.** With an odd number of flips there is never a tie, and by symmetry
"more heads" and "more tails" are equally likely.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Discrete mathematics, graphs and number theory
title: Q20, a remainder
stem: What is the remainder when $2^{100}$ is divided by 101?
answer: **(a) 1.** 101 is prime, so by Fermat $2^{100} \equiv 1 \pmod{101}$.

subject: Operating systems
title: Q21, starvation
stem: Which scheduling algorithms can cause starvation? (more than one answer)
answer:
**(a) and (b).** A stream of short jobs can postpone a long one forever. Round robin
gives every process a slice in turn.

subject: Operating systems
title: Q22, thrashing
stem: Which of these reduce thrashing? (more than one answer)
answer:
**(a) and (b).** Both give each process room for its working set. Page size does not
fix a working-set shortage.

options: Divide by zero exception at runtime
answer:
**(a) 2.** Textual expansion: `3 + 3 / 3 - 3` $= 3 + 1 - 3 = 1$, so $y = 1$ and
`ADD(y)` is $y + y = 2$. No division by zero ever happens.

subject: C programming

answer:
**(a) At least 12.** C89's translation limits require support for at least 12
pointer, array and function declarators modifying a type; compilers may allow more.

title: Q39, new versus malloc
stem: Select all true statements.
options: new calls the constructor while malloc does not
new is an operator while malloc is a function
new can be overloaded while malloc cannot
new returns the exact data type while malloc returns void*

**(a)-(d).** (e) is backwards: `new` throws `std::bad_alloc` and
`malloc` returns `NULL`.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q41, name mangling

called from C.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q42, conversion constructors
stem: Which are true about conversion constructors in C++? (more than one answer)
options: They can convert the data types of public variables
A conversion constructor accepts one argument of a different type
Conversion constructors do not exist in C++
A conversion constructor can do the job of the destructor
answer:
**(b).** A constructor callable with a single argument of another type (and not
`explicit`) is used for implicit conversions, e.g. `A a = 5;`.

MATLAB reports "Undefined function or variable `my_func`". Which will NOT resolve

Add the folder to the operating system path
Add the folder to the MATLAB path

**(b) 6.** A nested function shares the parent's workspace, so it sets the same
`x` to 5, and then $x + 1 = 6$.

Which commands remove the third row of a $3 \times 3$ matrix `A`, leaving

options: x3 is a cell array with 3 elements

**(c) only.** Parentheses index a cell array and return cells: `x1` and
`x2` are $1 \times 1$ cells (braces `A{1}` would give the contents), `x3`
is $1 \times 3$, and `n` is 5.

subject: Other
title: Q49, changing the loop variable
stem:
How many times is MATLAB printed?

```matlab
for k = 1:4
    if k == 2
        k = 5;
    end
    disp('MATLAB')
end
```
answer:
**4 times.** Assigning to `k` inside the loop changes it only for the rest of that
iteration; the next iteration takes the next value of `1:4`.

subject: Other
title: Q50, function precedence
stem:
Order by MATLAB's precedence (highest first): (1) nested functions, (2) imported
functions, (3) functions in the current folder, (4) private functions.
answer:
**(c) 2 1 4 3.** MATLAB's order is: variables, explicitly imported names, nested
functions, local functions, private functions, class methods and constructors, the
current folder, then the rest of the path.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q4, a Fibonacci lottery
stem:
In a lottery, 7 numbers are drawn without replacement from the first 20 Fibonacci numbers.
What is the probability that the first number is even and the second is od[d]? [cut off in the source]
answer:
**(c) 0.239**, counting from $F_0 = 0$: $F_0..F_{19}$ has 7 even and 13 odd numbers,
and $\frac{7}{20} \cdot \frac{13}{19} = 91/380 \approx 0.239$. (Starting from $F_1 = 1$
gives 6 even and $84/380 = 0.221$, which is not an option.)

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q5, a die ten times
stem: A die is rolled 10 times. The probability that 2 appears exactly 4 times is:
answer: **(a)**, the binomial probability with $n = 10$, $k = 4$, $p = 1/6$.

topic: Discrete mathematics, graphs and number theory
title: Q6, digit sum of a power of two
stem: The sum of the digits of $2^{100}$ is:
answer:
**(b) 7**, read as the repeated digit sum (digital root): $2^{100} \bmod 9$, with
$2^6 \equiv 1$, is $2^4 = 16 \equiv 7$. The plain digit sum is 115 (computed), which is not
an option.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming

answer:
**(b)** (tested: `sizeof` is 1). Every object needs a distinct address, so an
empty class has non-zero size. The candidate's "compilation error" is wrong.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: Q9, = ALL on an empty set
stem:
Table $R(A, B, C)$ (top rows [cut off in the source]; visible rows (8,5,6), (4,5,6), (3,4,5), (7,2,9)).
How many rows does

```sql
SELECT *
FROM R
WHERE C = ALL (SELECT B FROM R WHERE A > 10)
```

return?
answer:
**All the rows**, if no row has $A > 10$: `= ALL` over an empty subquery is true.
With the four visible rows that is **(c) 4** \unverified; the candidate's 0 is the
usual trap.

stem: The least time to find the first missing positive integer with $O(1)$ extra space is:
answer:
\textbf{(c) $O(n)$}: place each value $v \in [1, n]$ at index $v - 1$ by swapping, then scan.
The candidate's $O(n \log n)$ is wrong.

title: Q11, linear Diophantine equations
stem: For $ax + by = c$ with $g = \gcd(a, b)$ dividing $c$, the solutions for $x$ are:
answer:
**(b).** Divide by $g$: $(a/g)x \equiv c/g \pmod{b/g}$, and $a/g$ is invertible
modulo $b/g$.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q22, deleting through a base pointer
stem:
`Base` and `Derived` print "Constructing ..." in their constructors and
"Destroying ..." in their destructors; `Base`'s destructor is *not* virtual.

```cpp
Base *b = new Derived();
delete b;
```

What does this print? (CB = Constructing Base, etc.)
answer:
**(d) CB CD DB.** Construction goes base first. `delete` through a
`Base*` with a non-virtual destructor calls only `\textasciitilde Base`
(formally undefined behaviour); `Derived`'s destructor is skipped, which is why base
destructors should be virtual.

subject: C programming
title: Q24, dangling pointers
stem: A dangling pointer arises when:
options: the memory it points to is freed
answer:
**(d).** The pointer still holds the address of released memory. An uninitialised
pointer is a "wild" pointer.

(implementation-defined), while the `unsigned char` view is 128. Where `char`
is unsigned (e.g. ARM Linux) it prints 128 128.

answer:
**(c) 8 calls of printf** (the intended count). The first `fork` gives 2

Then all 4 print the last one: $2 + 2 + 4 = 8$. On a real system the first `*` is
still in the (unflushed) stdout buffer when the second `fork` copies it, so 10
characters actually appear. (d) is right in practice \unverified.

Three machines move along a circular track of 360 m at 37, 45 and 57 metres per minute.

lap: every $360/8 = 45$ min for the pair (37, 45) and every $360/12 = 30$ min for

divides 90 as well). The handwritten key leaves this one blank.
