subject: Software engineering and web
title: article view counts and categories in the Conduit app
stem:
You are given a working copy of *Conduit*, a Medium-like blogging site. It has an
Express.js back end using the Sequelize ORM and providing a REST API, and a React front
end. Users can sign up and log in, create, edit and delete markdown articles, comment,
follow other users, favourite articles, and filter articles by tag. The database is
seeded with 2 users and 7 articles. Implement four progressive features, each building on
the previous one.

1. **Tier 1, read-only API endpoint for article view count** (back end only).
    Add an integer `viewCount` attribute to the Article model, with default 0.
    Create an API route `/articles/:slug/viewed` that increments the counter when an
    article is viewed. Return `viewCount` with the article data.
2. **Tier 2, display the view count in the UI** (front end only). Every time an
    article is viewed, call the tier-1 API to increment the value by 1. Show a small icon
    and the `viewCount` value (for example "42 views") below the article title.
3. **Tier 3, article categories.** Implement article categories, separate from
    tags. Create a new Category model with attributes for name and description
    [cut off in the source].
4. Tier 4 is not visible in the photos.

Outline how you would implement tiers 1 to 3.
answer:
**Tier 1 (back end).**

- Add a migration with `viewCount INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` on the articles
    table, and declare it in the model. Since `rebuild-database.sh` re-seeds,
    existing rows get 0.
- Add `router.route("/:slug/viewed").put(articleViewed)` (or `POST`).
    It changes state, so it should not be a `GET`. Decide deliberately whether it
    sits behind the `protect` middleware: anonymous readers count as views too.
- In the controller, find the article by slug (404 if it is missing), then
    increment it *atomically* in the database with
    `await article.increment("viewCount")`. This issues
    `UPDATE ...{} SET viewCount = viewCount + 1`, so concurrent views are not lost,
    unlike read-modify-save. Then `reload()` and return the article.
- Make sure the article serialiser (the `toJSON` or the response mapper used by
    `getArticle` and `getArticles`) includes `viewCount`.

**Tier 2 (front end).** In the article page component, call the endpoint once per
view, in a `useEffect` keyed on the slug. In React's development StrictMode, effects
run twice, so guard with a ref if double counting matters. Store the returned count in
state, and render it under the title with an eye icon, for example
`{viewCount} views`. No back-end changes are needed.

**Tier 3 (categories).**

- Add a `Category` model (`id`, unique `name`, `description`)
    with its migration.
- Relate it to articles. Either use `Article.belongsTo(Category)` with a
    `categoryId` foreign key (one category per article, unlike tags), or a join table
    if several categories per article are wanted.
- Add CRUD routes `/categories`, accept `categoryId` in the
    create/update-article payload with validation, include the category in article
    responses, and support `?category=` filtering in `getArticles`, alongside
    the existing `tag` filter.
- On the front end, add a category select in the editor and a category filter on
    the home feed.

Keep categories separate from tags in both the schema and the API, as the task requires.

subject: Operating systems
title: process information
stem: The operating system maintains the information about a process in which of the following?
answer:
**(b) Process Control Block**: process id, state, registers and program counter,
scheduling, memory and I/O information.

subject: Operating systems
title: why "virtual" memory
stem: Why is a virtual memory address called "virtual"?
options: This memory address does not map to the actual memory cell that corresponds to the address number.
This memory is the same as physical memory.
This memory cannot be accessed by applications at run time.
This memory address is always present even after a system is restarted.
answer:
**(a).** The MMU translates it through page tables to some physical frame (or it may
not be in RAM at all), so the number is not the physical location.

subject: C programming
title: MAX macro with side effects
stem: What does this program print?
answer:
**(a) 11 6 12** is the intended answer (and what gcc prints). The macro expands to
`((x++) > (y++) ? (x++) : (y++))`: $5 > 10$ is false, so $y$ is incremented a second
time and the expression yields 11; $x$ ends at 6 and $y$ at 12. Strictly, the call is
undefined behaviour: `x` and `y` are modified in one argument and read in
others with no sequence point between them (gcc warns "operation on x may be
undefined"). (Compiled and run.)

subject: Java
topic: Algorithms and output prediction in Java
title: recursive swap
options: The sum of all the elements of the array
The product of all the elements in the array
The last element of the array
Reverses the contents of the array.
answer:
**(d) It reverses `data[low..high]`**, swapping the two ends and recursing
inwards.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: range-partitioned table
stem:
A table `orders` has columns `order_id` (primary key), `customer_id`,
`order_date` and `total_amount`. Which SQL statement correctly creates a table
partitioned by range on `order_date`? (Each option is abbreviated to its partition
clause.)
options: partition by range columns (order_date) (partition p1 values less than ('2023-01-01') tablespace ts1, partition p2 values less than ('2024-01-01') tablespace ts2);
partition by range (order_date) (partition p1 ..., partition p2 ...) primary key (order_id);
partition by range (order_date) (partition p1 values less than ('2023-01-01') tablespace ts1, partition p2 values less than ('2024-01-01') tablespace ts2);
partition by range (order_date) (partition p1 ..., partition p2 ...) partition by range (order_id);
answer:
**(c).** Oracle's syntax is

```cpp
PARTITION BY RANGE (col) (PARTITION p VALUES LESS THAN (...) TABLESPACE t, ...)
```

`RANGE COLUMNS` is MySQL syntax; a primary key
clause cannot follow the partition list; and a table has one partitioning clause (two-level
schemes use `SUBPARTITION BY`). (In real Oracle the bounds would be written as dates,
e.g. `DATE '2023-01-01'` or `TO_DATE(...)`.)

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: key-value store

subject: DBMS and SQL

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: when not to use NoSQL
stem:
Which of the following design criteria is not valid/suitable for (choosing) non-relational
databases?
options: Your data are unstructured without any relation between them
You only need to serialize and deserialize data (JSON, XML, YAML)
You need to store a very small amount of data
answer:
**(d).** The usual reasons to pick NoSQL are very low latency, unstructured data,
simple serialisation of objects, and *massive* amounts of data; a very small amount of
data is not a reason.

subject: DBMS and SQL

Which clause restricts the groups of rows returned to those groups for which the specified

**(b) HAVING**, which filters after `GROUP BY`; `WHERE` filters rows before

subject: Software engineering and web
title: CAP theorem
stem: What does the CAP theorem describe with respect to system design?
options: The relationship between CPU and memory usage
The trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
answer:
**(b).** A distributed store cannot guarantee all three at once; during a network
partition it must give up consistency or availability.

subject: Software engineering and web
title: idempotency in REST
stem: What does idempotency mean in REST API design?
options: The ability of an API to handle multiple requests in parallel
The property that a method can be called multiple times without different outcomes
The capability of an API to update data
The feature of an API that allows it to delete resources
answer: **(b).** GET, PUT, DELETE (and HEAD, OPTIONS) are idempotent; POST is not.

It contains a list of all files in the system
It contains the time and date information.

subject: Computer networks
title: ring topology failure
stem: In a ring topology network, if one device fails, how does it affect the network?
options: Only the failed device is affected
All devices in the network are affected
Only the devices between which the failed device exists are affected
The network continues to function normally
answer:
**(b).** In a simple (single, unidirectional) ring every message passes through every
node, so one failure breaks the whole ring. Dual rings such as FDDI can wrap around a
failure, but that is not the textbook answer.

subject: Computer networks
title: ARP

options: To convert IP addresses to MAC addresses
To convert domain names to IP addresses
To establish a secure connection between client and server
answer: **(a).** DNS does (b), TLS (c), routers and routing protocols (d).

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: symmetric sparse matrix
stem: In what way can a symmetric sparse matrix be stored efficiently?
answer:
**(d) Adjacency list** \unverified. A symmetric sparse matrix is the adjacency matrix of
an undirected sparse graph, and storing only the non-zero entries per row (an adjacency list,
i.e. compressed rows, keeping just one triangle) uses $O(\text{non-zeros})$ space. A hash
table keyed by $(i, j)$ also works, but it is not the classic answer.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: 2-3 tree versus BST
stem: Which of the following is false?
options: 2-3 tree requires less storage than the BST
lookup in 2-3 tree is more efficient than in BST
answer:
**(a).** 3-nodes hold two keys and three child pointers, so a 2-3 tree generally needs
*more* storage for the same keys. Being balanced (all leaves at one depth), it is
shallower than an arbitrary BST and has guaranteed $O(\log n)$ lookup.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: recipe ingredients
stem:
The ingredients are apricots, bacon, cake, donuts, eggs, figs, grapes, hazelnuts and ice
cream. (1) If bacon is not used, then grapes, hazelnuts and ice cream are not used. (2) If
apricots are used then bacon and cake are used. (3) If donuts are not used, apricots are not
used. (4) Apricots and eggs are used. [cut off in the source] (the question line is off screen; the
options suggest "what is the minimum number of ingredients used?")
answer:
**(d) 5**, under the assumed question. Apricots and eggs are used (4); apricots force
bacon and cake (2); by the contrapositive of (3) apricots force donuts. Nothing else is forced,
so the minimum is apricots, eggs, bacon, cake, donuts.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: painted cube
stem:
A cube is painted green on all surfaces and cut into 1000 identical cubes. How many of the
smaller cubes have three faces painted?
answer: **(a) 8**: only the corner cubes, whatever the size.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: road network, where does the journey end
stem:
There is a network of eight cities (vertices) connected by roads. A traveller must drive on
each road segment once, but can visit a city multiple times if necessary; the start and end
points need not match. New roads are constructed between $C$ and $G$, and between $H$ and $F$.
If the journey begins at $B$, where will it end?
[figure: see the original PDF]
(Figure redrawn from the video frames; the new roads $C$-$G$ and $H$-$F$ are added to it.)
answer:
**(a) E.** A walk that uses every road exactly once (an Euler path) must start and end
at the two vertices of odd degree. With the two new roads the degrees are
$A{:}2, B{:}3, C{:}4, D{:}2, E{:}3, F{:}4, G{:}4, H{:}4$, so starting at $B$ the journey
ends at $E$. The photo ticks $G$, which has even degree and cannot be an end point.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: five people, sports and colours
stem:
Jack, Matthew, Albert, Peter and Sebastian each play one of football, cricket, volleyball,
badminton and squash; are from South Korea, the UK, India, China and Russia; and have
favourite colours brown, green, red, black and yellow (all different).
(1) Jack's favourite colour is red; he is not from India or China. (2) Albert plays football;
his favourite colour is not yellow and he is not from the UK. (3) Peter and Sebastian have
yellow and green as favourite colours, in some order. (4) Matthew plays badminton; he is from
Russia. (5) Peter and Sebastian are from China and the UK, in some order. (6) Brown is the
favourite colour of the person from India. (7) Green is the favourite colour of the person
from China. (8) The person from South Korea plays squash and the person from the UK plays
volleyball; one of them has yellow as favourite colour.
Whose favourite colour is black?
answer:
**(a) Matthew.** Peter and Sebastian take China and the UK, Matthew Russia, and Jack
cannot be Indian, so Jack is South Korean and Albert Indian (brown). Red, brown, yellow and
green are then taken, leaving black for Matthew. (An exhaustive search finds two complete
solutions, differing only in how Peter and Sebastian share China/UK; Matthew is black in
both.) The photo ticks Albert, whose colour is brown.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: standing order

Peter, Tyson, Richard, Steve and Quinn stand in a row. (1) Peter is next to Quinn and Steve
is next to Richard. (2) Steve is not next to Tyson. (3) Tyson is in the leftmost position.
(4) Richard is second from the right. (5) Peter stands somewhere to the right of both Quinn
and Tyson. (6) Peter and Richard are next to each other. Who is in the middle?
answer:
**(a) Peter.** The only order is Tyson, Quinn, Peter, Richard, Steve (found by
exhaustive search).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: sports enthusiasts
stem:
In a company, 100 employees are randomly selected. 50 like watching football, 40 like
watching hockey and the rest like both. Find the number of employees who like to watch at
least one of the games.
answer:
**(c) 80**, the intended key: reading 50 and 40 as totals and the "rest",
$100 - 50 - 40 = 10$, as those liking both gives $50 + 40 - 10 = 80$. The wording is
inconsistent: if everyone likes something, the answer would be 100, which is not offered.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: only cricket
stem:
In a group of students, 60% like football and 40% like cricket. What percentage of students
like only cricket if 12% like neither football nor cricket?
answer:
**(a) 28.** $88\%$ like at least one, so both $= 60 + 40 - 88 = 12\%$, and only cricket
$= 40 - 12 = 28\%$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude

stem: What is the remainder of 1992 divided by 92?
answer: **(d) None of the above**: $1992 = 21 \cdot 92 + 60$, remainder 60.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: phone brands, data interpretation
stem:
Customers (in millions) using each brand of phone, and customers added in each month (Euphore
has two versions):
|  | Customers | Added in the month |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Month | Hington | Euphore | Hington | Euphore V1 | Euphore V2 |
| Aug-12 | 46.18 | 47.28 | 0.36 | 1.24 | 0.6 |
| Sep-12 | 47.34 | 48.91 | 1.16 | 1.08 | 0.8 |
| Oct-12 | 49.32 | 49.27 | 1.98 | 0.84 | 0.48 |
What was the total number of people using either of the two brands in July 2012?
(Transcribed from video frames; some digits are blurred.)
answer:
**(a) 91.21 million** \unverified. July is August minus August's additions:
Hington $46.18 - 0.36 = 45.82$ and Euphore $47.28 - (1.24 + 0.6) = 45.44$, total 91.26 with
the digits as read. The nearest option, 91.21 (ticked), is almost certainly the key, so one
blurred digit (probably Hington's 0.36, which would be 0.41) is misread.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Group Membership 3, three languages
stem:
A survey of 300 people was taken. Given the results, find how many people speak all
three languages: 85% speak English, 40% Spanish and 20% French; 32% speak both
English and Spanish, 13% both English and French, and 10% both Spanish and French.
answer:
**(a) 30.** By inclusion-exclusion, the share speaking at least one language is
$85 + 40 + 20 - 32 - 13 - 10 + x = 90 + x$ percent, where $x$ is the share speaking all
three. Every surveyed person speaks at least one of them, which is the assumption the
question intends, so $90 + x = 100$ and $x = 10\%$, that is, $30$ people. (Option (c),
10, is the percentage, not the number of people.)

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: List Customer and Product Without Sale
stem:
Tables: `customer(id, customer_name, city_id, customer_address, contact_person,
email, phone)`; `product(id, sku, product_name, product_description,
current_price, quantity_in_stock)`; `invoice(id, invoice_number, customer_id,
user_account_id, total_price, time_issued, time_due, time_paid, time_canceled,
time_refunded)`, where `customer_id` references `customer.id`; and
`invoice_item(id, invoice_id, product_id, quantity, price, line_total_price)`,
referencing `invoice` and `product`.

Using the `UNION` operator, return in one list all customers who do not have an
invoice and all products that were not sold. For each such customer return the string
`customer`, the customer id and the `customer_name`; for each such product the
string `product`, the product id and the `product_name`. The columns must be in
this order, but row order does not matter. The expected result starts with the line
`customer 2 Cosmetics Store`.
answer:
```sql
SELECT 'customer' AS category, c.id, c.customer_name AS name
FROM customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoice i WHERE i.customer_id = c.id)
UNION
SELECT 'product', p.id, p.product_name
FROM product p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoice_item ii WHERE ii.product_id = p.id);
```

`NOT EXISTS` (or a `LEFT JOIN ...{} WHERE i.id IS NULL`) is safe with
`NULL`s, unlike `NOT IN` over a column that may contain `NULL`. The two
branches must have the same number of columns, which is why a constant string is
selected. `UNION` removes duplicate rows; `UNION ALL` would do here as well,
since the two branches can never produce the same row.

Run in SQLite on the sample rows that are legible in the photos (9 customers, 10 products,
6 invoices, 9 invoice items), it returns customers 1, 2 and 8 and products 3, 6, 8 and 9.
The real sample has more invoice rows than the photos show, which explains why the
expected output starts with customer 2.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: inorder traversal
stem:
What is the inorder traversal of this tree? Root F; F's children are B and G; B's are A
and D; D's are C and E; G has only a right child I, whose only child is its left child H.
answer:
**(b) ABCDEFGHI.** Left subtree $A, B, C, D, E$, then $F$, then the right subtree:
$G$, then $I$'s left child $H$, then $I$. Inorder traversal of a binary search tree on
letters gives sorted order, which is a quick check. Option (a) is the preorder and (c)
the postorder.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Convert an Expression, maximum stack length
stem:
What is the maximum length of the stack when converting the infix expression
$(a-b)*c/(d/f-g)*h$ to postfix?
answer:
**(c) 3.** Only operators and parentheses go on the stack (shunting-yard). `( -`
is 2 deep, then `)` empties it. `*` is pushed, and `/` pops it (equal
precedence, left-associative) and is pushed. Then `/ (` and `/ ( /` reach 3.
`-` pops the inner `/` and gives `/ ( -`, again 3. `)` unwinds to
`/`, and the last `*` replaces it. The maximum is 3.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Max Stack
stem:
Find the maximum length the stack will have when performing: Push(10); Pop();
Push(17); Push(29); Push(6); Pop(); Push(10); Push(77); Pop();
answer:
**(c) 4.** The sizes after each operation are 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4, 3, reaching 4
after Push(77).

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Critical MST edges
stem:
A critical MST edge is an edge whose deletion would increase the weight of the minimum
spanning tree; if deleting it disconnects the graph, the MST weight becomes infinite. The
graph has edges $0\!-\!1$ (2), $1\!-\!2$ (2), $2\!-\!3$ (1), $3\!-\!4$ (5), $0\!-\!4$ (5)
and $4\!-\!5$ (5). Which of the following are critical edges? (Pick one or more.)
answer:
**(a) and (d).** The MST weight is $1 + 2 + 2 + 5 + 5 = 15$: the three light edges
on the cycle, *one* of the two weight-5 edges $3\!-\!4$ and $0\!-\!4$, and
$4\!-\!5$.

- Removing $0\!-\!1$ forces both weight-5 cycle edges into the tree: 18, so it is
    critical.
- $4\!-\!5$ is a bridge: removing it disconnects the graph, so it is critical.
- $3\!-\!4$ and $0\!-\!4$ can replace each other, so neither is critical.

($1\!-\!2$ and $2\!-\!3$ are critical too, but they are not among the options.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: postorder from inorder and preorder
stem:
Given the inorder and preorder traversals of a tree, find its postorder traversal.
Inorder: $[9, 2, 4, 6, 8, 7, 3, 1, 5, 10]$. Preorder: $[8, 2, 9, 6, 4, 1, 3, 7, 5, 10]$.
answer:
**(b).** The root is 8 (first in preorder). Its left inorder part $[9, 2, 4, 6]$
has preorder $[2, 9, 6, 4]$: root 2, left child 9, right child 6, whose left child is
4. So the left subtree's postorder is $9, 4, 6, 2$. The right part $[7, 3, 1, 5, 10]$
has preorder $[1, 3, 7, 5, 10]$: root 1, left 3 (with left child 7), right 5 (with right
child 10). So the right subtree's postorder is $7, 3, 10, 5, 1$. The whole postorder is
$[9, 4, 6, 2, 7, 3, 10, 5, 1, 8]$.

One photo ticks (c), which swaps 7 and 3: 7 is 3's *child*, so 7 must come first.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: top and bottom of the stack
stem:
In the postfix expression `6 3 2 * / 3 2 1 * - +`, what are the values of the top
and the bottom of the stack just before the second `*` is performed?
answer:
**(a) 1, 1.** Push 6, 3, 2; the first `*` gives $3 \cdot 2 = 6$, so the stack
is $[6, 6]$; `/` gives $6 / 6 = 1$, so it is $[1]$. Pushing 3, 2, 1 gives
$[1, 3, 2, 1]$, and the second `*` sees top 1 and bottom 1.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Number of Swaps II
stem:
Find the minimum number of swaps required to convert
`arr1 = [7, 6, 1, 3, 4, 9, 8, 2, 5]` into `arr2 = [3, 1, 8, 5, 4, 9, 2, 6, 7]`.
answer:
**(b) 5.** Map every position of `arr1` to where its value must go in
`arr2`. The resulting permutation has cycles $(0\,8\,3)$, $(1\,7\,6\,2)$, $(4)$ and
$(5)$. A cycle of length $L$ needs $L - 1$ swaps, so the total is $n - \#\text{cycles} = 9
- 4 = 5$.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: DFS-4, valid depth-first orders
stem:
Which of the paths is or are valid for a depth-first search from node 0? The graph has
edges $0\!-\!5$, $0\!-\!4$, $0\!-\!2$, $2\!-\!3$, $5\!-\!7$, $5\!-\!6$, $5\!-\!1$,
$1\!-\!8$ and $1\!-\!4$. (Pick one or more.)
answer:
**(b) only.** In a DFS, the next vertex must be an unvisited neighbour of the
deepest vertex on the current path that still has one.

- (a) is wrong: after 0, 2 the search must go to 3 (2's unvisited neighbour)
    before anything else.
- (b) works: $0 \to 5 \to 6$, back to 5, $\to 7$, back, $\to 1 \to 8$, back to 1,
    $\to 4$; then back to 0, $\to 2 \to 3$.
- (c) visits 3 straight after 4, but 3 is adjacent only to 2.
- (d) is wrong: after 8 the search backtracks to 1, which still has the unvisited
    neighbour 4, so the next vertex must be 4, not 2.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: trailing zeros
stem: What is the smallest $N$ such that $N!$ ends in exactly 100 zeros?
answer:
**405.** The number of trailing zeros of $N!$ is
$Z(N) = \floor{N/5} + \floor{N/25} + \floor{N/125} + \cdots$, the number of factors 5.
$Z(400) = 80 + 16 + 3 = 99$, and $Z$ jumps at the next multiple of 5:
$Z(405) = 81 + 16 + 3 = 100$. (Checked by computing $Z(N)$ for all $N$.)
Note that some counts are skipped: $Z$ jumps by 2 or more at multiples of 25,
so for some targets no $N$ exists.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: mathematicians in rooms
stem: $N$ mathematicians and $k$ rooms: in how many ways can they arrange themselves?
answer:
\unverified{} The recorded statement does not say whether rooms may stay empty or
whether rooms are distinguishable, so here are the standard readings:

- distinct rooms, rooms may be empty: each mathematician picks a room,
    $k^N$ ways;
- distinct rooms, no room empty: $k!\,S(N, k)$, where $S(N,k)$ is a Stirling
    number of the second kind (inclusion-exclusion:
    $\sum_{i=0}^{k} (-1)^i \binom{k}{i} (k-i)^N$);
- identical rooms, none empty: $S(N, k)$.

Without further conditions the expected answer is $k^N$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: coin game with a doubling option
stem:
You and a friend toss a fair coin repeatedly. On heads you gain 1 point and your
friend loses 1; on tails your friend gains 1 point and you lose 1. The game ends when
a player reaches 2 points; that player wins and the other pays the winner \$10.

1. What is the expected value of the game for each player at the start?
2. At any point you may, once, raise the prize from \$10 to \$20. What is the
    optimal strategy, and what is the expected value of the game under it?
answer:
**Part 1: \$0 for both.** Your score $s$ does a symmetric random walk from 0,
and the game ends at $s = \pm 2$; by symmetry each player wins with probability
$\tfrac12$.

\textbf{Part 2: raise the stake the first time you are ahead ($s = 1$); your
expected value is \$$10/3 \approx 3.33$ (your friend's is $-\$3.33$).}
From $s$, you win with probability $(s + 2)/4$ (gambler's ruin on $\{-2, \dots, 2\}$).
At $s = 1$ that is $\tfrac34$, so raising gives $20 \cdot \tfrac34 - 20 \cdot \tfrac14
= 10$, while waiting gives at most $\tfrac12 \cdot 10 + \tfrac12 V(0) < 10$.
At $s \le 0$ raising has value $\le 0$, so you wait. With $V(1) = 10$,
$V(-1) = \tfrac12 V(0) - 5$ and $V(0) = \tfrac12 V(1) + \tfrac12 V(-1)$, which gives
$V(0) = 10/3$. (Checked by value iteration.)

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: guessing n
stem:
A number is chosen uniformly at random from $1, 2, \dots, n$ and it turns out to be
50. What is the best guess for $n$?
answer:
It depends on what "best" means, and interviewers usually want both answers:

- \textbf{Maximum likelihood: $n = 50$.} The probability of seeing 50 is $1/n$
    for $n \ge 50$ (and 0 below), which is largest at $n = 50$.
- \textbf{Unbiased estimate: $n = 99$.} For one draw $X$,
    $\EE[X] = (n+1)/2$, so $2X - 1$ is unbiased: $2 \cdot 50 - 1 = 99$
    (the one-sample case of the German tank problem).

subject: Python
title: Q27, Marines at your positions (pandas)
answer:
**Use `iloc`.** It selects by *position*. Plain `s[list_pos]` relies
on the index labels happening to equal the positions, and recent pandas versions warn
about or reject positional use of `[]`.

```python
import pandas as pd
list_input = input().split()
list_pos = list(map(int, input().split()))
s = pd.Series(list_input)
print(s.iloc[list_pos])
```

For the sample this prints the index-value pairs `0 a`, `4 e`, `8 i`,
`14 o` and `20 u`, one per line, followed by the dtype line. That line is
`dtype: object` in pandas 1.x and 2.x; pandas 3.0, which was used to run this
answer, prints `dtype: str`. All values are read as strings. The test used Python 2,
where `raw_input` replaces `input`.

subject: DBMS and SQL
title: top sale in the Electronics department
stem:
Tables `employees(emp_id, name, department)` and `sales(emp_id, amount,
date)`. The question text is outside the photo; the candidate's answer, shown below,
reports the Electronics employee or employees with the largest sale amount:

```sql
SELECT emp_id, name, amount
FROM (
  SELECT s.emp_id, e.name, s.amount,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s.amount DESC) AS rnk
  FROM sales s
  JOIN employees e ON e.emp_id = s.emp_id
  WHERE e.department = 'Electronics') t
WHERE rnk = 1;
```

What does this query return, and how would it change if the question asked for the
employee with the largest *total* sales?
answer:
**What it returns.** The join keeps the sales made by Electronics employees.
`RANK()` orders them by amount, with ties sharing rank 1, so the outer filter returns
every sale whose amount equals the maximum, together with the seller's id and name.
`RANK` rather than `ROW_NUMBER` is right if ties should all be reported. The
filter on `rnk` must sit in an outer query, because a window function cannot be
used in `WHERE` at the same level. An employee with two equal top sales would appear
twice.

**Largest total per employee.** Aggregate first, then rank:

```sql
SELECT emp_id, name, total
FROM (SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, SUM(s.amount) AS total,
             RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(s.amount) DESC) AS rnk
      FROM sales s JOIN employees e ON e.emp_id = s.emp_id
      WHERE e.department = 'Electronics'
      GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.name) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
```

subject: Logical reasoning
title: mother scolds, hide or complain
stem:
Read the scenario and determine the logical link between the conditions and the options.
"Whenever my mother scolds me, I either hide behind my father or complain to my grandma."
options: If I complain to my grandma or I hide behind my father, then my mother must have scolded me.
If I did not complain to my grandma and I did not hide behind my father, then my mother must not have scolded me.
If my mother does not scold me, I will neither hide behind my father nor complain to my grandma.
None of the mentioned options are correct.
answer:
**(b).** The statement is $S \Rightarrow (H \lor C)$. Its contrapositive,
$\lnot H \land \lnot C \Rightarrow \lnot S$, is equivalent to it, and that is option (b).
Option (a) is the converse and option (c) is the inverse; neither follows from the
statement.

title: Q44, unpipelined latency
stem:
An unpipelined processor with 5 stages has execution stages of 90 ns, 70 ns, 10 ns, 40 ns
and 130 ns. What is the instruction latency of the unpipelined stage? (Assume an overhead of
5 ns.)
answer:
**(b) 340 ns** \unverified. Without pipelining an instruction passes through all stages:
$90 + 70 + 10 + 40 + 130 = 340$ ns; the 5 ns latch overhead belongs to the pipelined design,
whose clock would be $130 + 5 = 135$ ns (option (c)). If the question means to add one
overhead, 345 is the other reading.

Process Next (SPN) is on the higher side compared to FCFS. (II) The overhead of Round Robin is

answer:
**(d) Only (I) and (II)** (Stallings' comparison table: SPN throughput high; RR overhead
minimum, SPN overhead can be high). FCFS never starves a process: everyone is served in turn.

title: Q59, proportional frame allocation
stem:
There are 55 frames to be divided between two processes P1 and P2; P1 has 17 pages and P2

title: Q58, balancing a BST
stem:
Construct a BST from $40, 30, 25, 45, 50, 19, 27$. Which node(s) should be deleted to make the
resulting BST balanced?
answer:
**(d) 30.** The tree is 40 with left 30 (whose left child 25 has children 19, 27) and
right 45 (right child 50). Node 30 is unbalanced (left height 2, right 0). Deleting 30 lets 25
take its place with children 19 and 27, and every node is then balanced. (Deleting 30 and 27
also gives a balanced tree, but one deletion suffices; deleting 50 makes the root unbalanced.)
