subject: Logical reasoning
title: circular seating (1)
stem:
Six people, Sonu, Monu, Jim, Akash, Anvesha and Kapil, sit around a circular table facing the
centre. Anvesha is not sitting between Monu and Akash. Some people are sitting between Monu and
Akash. Sonu sits just left of Kapil. Jim is fourth to the right of Sonu.
Who sits second to the right of Sonu?
answer:
**(d) Anvesha.** Going clockwise (each person's left): Sonu, Monu/Akash, Jim,
Akash/Monu, Anvesha, Kapil, with Jim the one person between Monu and Akash. The two
arrangements differ only by swapping Monu and Akash. Sonu's second to the right is Anvesha in
both. (Checked by enumerating all seatings.) The photo ticks Kapil, who is on Sonu's right.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: circular seating (2)
stem: Same arrangement as the previous question. Who sits exactly between Akash and Monu?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: circular seating (3)
stem: Same arrangement. Who sits second to the right of Kapil?
answer:
**(a) Either Akash or Monu**: the seat next to Anvesha on the other side, which Monu and
Akash can swap.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: circular seating (4)
stem: Same arrangement. Who sits second to the left of Sonu?
answer: **(a) Jim**, which is also given: fourth to the right of 6 seats is second to the left.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: circular seating (5)
stem: Same arrangement. Who is sitting opposite to Jim?
answer: **(a) Kapil** (three seats from Jim either way).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q9, same selling price
stem:
The selling prices of two articles are the same. In one transaction the trader made a
[cut off in the source] ... the entire transaction?
answer:
\unverified{} (the percentages are cut off). The rule: if two articles are sold at the same
price, one at a gain of $x\%$ and one at a loss of $x\%$, there is always a net
*loss* of $x^2/100$ percent; with unequal gain and loss percentages, compute each cost
price as $\text{SP}/(1 \pm p)$ and compare.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q11, number boxes
stem:
Which number replaces the question mark? Each box has numbers at its four corners
(top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) and a number inside:
$(3, 4, 2, 2) \to 30$; $(7, 4, 4, 5) \to 1217$; $(8, 4, 7, 5) \to 1589$; $(11, 6, 5, 7) \to\ ?$
answer:
\unverified{} I could not find the rule: a computer search over sums, differences, products
and squares of the corners, concatenated, fits none of the three boxes, so a corner number was
probably misread in the blurred photo. Attempt it as a practice puzzle.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: peculiar numbers
stem:
A four-digit number is called peculiar if the sum of the number formed by the first
[cut off in the source] ... numbers are arranged in ascending order, find the sum of peculiar numbers just
[cut off in the source].
answer: Not answerable: the definition of "peculiar" is cut off in the photo.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q12, team with at least two women
stem:
Out of 9 women and 6 men, a team of 3 is to be formed so that at least two members are women.
In how many ways can it be done?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: letter-number series
stem: What is the missing term? J7, T5, ___, N6, X9
answer:
**(b) D8.** Letters move 10 places each time (J $\to$ T $\to$ D $\to$ N $\to$ X,
wrapping after Z); the numbers alternate $7, 8, 9$ and $5, 6$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q18, distance of a particle
stem:
The distance covered by a particle in $t$ seconds consists of two parts, one of which varies
with $t$ and the other with $t^2$. If [cut off in the source] ..., what is the distance travelled in the
first three seconds?
answer:
\unverified{} (the given data is cut off). Method: write $s = at + bt^2$, find $a$ and $b$ from
the two given distances, then evaluate $s(3)$.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: octal to decimal
stem: What is the decimal equivalent of $(556)_8$?
options: Given number is not in octal format.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q3, water image
stem:
Which is the exact water image of the word POTATO? (The four options are drawings of the word
reflected or rotated; see the source photo.)
answer:
\unverified{} A water image reflects across a horizontal line: the letters stay in the same
order (P first) but each is flipped upside down. The option ticked in the photo (second) looks
like that; the options reversed left-to-right are mirror images.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q5, train and platform
stem:
A train travelling at 36 km/h crosses a platform in 50 seconds; the platform's length equals
the length of the train. Find the length (of the train) [cut off in the source].
answer: **(b) 250 metres**: 36 km/h $= 10$ m/s, so it covers 500 m $= 2L$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: branches pie chart
stem:
A pie chart gives the number of branches of a company by state (TN 16%, WB 22%, JH 20%,
MP 24%, UP 18%), and a second chart (partly visible) gives employees by state; all branches of
a state have the same employee strength. Three questions were asked: which state has the most
employees per branch (options MP, JH, TN, cannot be determined); a ratio question starting "If
MP has 1872 employees and UP has 9 branches ..."; and an office-area question for JH
(50{,}000 sq ft). The employee chart and the ends of the questions are [cut off in the source].
answer:
\unverified{} Not answerable from the photos: every question needs the employee percentages,
which are cut off. Method: employees per branch in a state
$= (\text{employee share}) / (\text{branch share})$, up to a common factor.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q4, Hitesh and Priya
stem:
Hitesh alone can complete a job in 18 days. Had Priya joined him 3 days after he started
working, they would have [cut off in the source]. If they started working together, in how many days would they
complete the work?
answer:
\unverified{} (the key sentence is cut off). The method: from the missing sentence find Priya's
rate $1/p$; together they need $1 / (1/18 + 1/p)$ days.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q6, selling at 2/5 of cost
stem:
The cost price of a book is Rs 350; it is sold at $2/5$ times the cost price. What is the
profit or loss percentage?
answer: **(a) 60% loss**: selling at 40% of cost.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q7, mixing alloys
stem:
In two alloys the ratio of iron to copper is $4:3$ and $6:1$. If 14 kg of the first alloy
[cut off in the source] ... alloy?
answer:
\unverified{} The usual version mixes 14 kg of the first with 42 kg of the second:
iron $8 + 36 = 44$, copper $6 + 6 = 12$, ratio $11:3$ (option (c)). The photo ticks $3:11$,
which is the ratio inverted.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q1, team with one officer
stem:
From 4 officers and 8 jawans, in how many ways can a team of six be chosen to include exactly
one officer?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Q2, letter pairs in CHORDAMESODERM
stem:
How many pairs of letters are there in the word CHORDAMESODERM which have as many letters
between them in the word as in the English alphabet?
answer:
**(b) 4**: H-M, D-M, O-R and D-E (checked by a program over all pairs, in both
directions). The photo ticks 6.

subject: Operating systems
title: Q31, release time of a process
stem:
Which one of the given options is also called the release time of a CPU scheduling
process?
answer:
**Ambiguous; most likely (b) Completion time is intended.** In real-time scheduling,
"release time" means the time a job becomes ready (its *arrival* time), which is not
an option. Question banks for this test equate it with the time the process leaves the
system, i.e. completion time. \unverified{}

subject: C programming
title: Q29, statements about pointers
stem:
Choose the correct statement(s). I) The address stored in a pointer variable is always of
type integer. II) A pointer is a variable that stores the address of another variable.
answer:
**(d) Only (II).** A pointer has a pointer type (`int*`, `char*`, ...), not
an integer type; converting it to an integer needs a cast (or `uintptr_t`).

subject: C programming
topic: General output prediction and compile errors
title: Q26, which line has an error
stem: Which of the line(s) generates error(s) in the program below?
answer:
**The error is in `++*ar += 1;`**, the unlabelled line above "Line 1": in C,
`++*ar` is not an lvalue, so it cannot be assigned to (GCC: "lvalue required as left
operand of assignment"). In C++ the same line compiles. The labelled lines are fine
(`array[!1]` is `array[0]`). If the setter's labels are shifted by one line, as
the options suggest, the intended answer is **(d) Line 1**.

subject: Operating systems
title: Q30, page stealing
stem: Which one of the given options is correct about page stealing?
options: It cleans up all the dirty pages.
It shows that the system is efficient.
It takes the page frames out and makes space for the newer page.
It takes the larger disk space for pages that are paged out.
answer:
**(c).** Page stealing takes frames away (often from other processes) to make room
for newly needed pages; frequent stealing signals memory pressure, not efficiency.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q27, accesses that reach main memory
stem:
A processor has an L1 and an L2 cache with hit rates 0.58 and 0.76 respectively. What
fraction of the memory accesses reach main memory?
answer:
**(d) 0.1008** $= (1 - 0.58)(1 - 0.76) = 0.42 \times 0.24$: an access goes to memory
only if it misses both caches (the L2 hit rate is local, among L1 misses).

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q23, intersection law in Boolean logic
stem:
Which equation(s) are correct for the intersection law in Boolean logic?
I) $P \cdot 1 = 0$. II) $P \cdot 1 = P$. III) $P \cdot 0 = P$. IV) $P \cdot 0 = 0$.
answer: **(c) (II) and (IV)**: 1 is the identity for AND, and 0 annihilates.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: subjects chart, boys in 2012
stem:
A bar graph shows the number of students (in hundreds) who chose Science, Maths, English and
Hindi: 2010: 20, 34, 54, 33; 2011: 34, 67, 36, 45; 2012: 12, 46, 44, 30; 2013: 46, 36, 24,
47; 2014: 35, 36, 30, 20; 2016: 32, 27, 52, 40 (the 2016 Science and Maths bars are hard to
separate). How many boys chose at least one of the subjects in 2012, if 25% of the students
in 2012 were girls?
answer:
**(d) 9900**, assuming each student chose one subject: 2012 total
$= 12 + 46 + 44 + 30 = 132$ hundred $= 13200$, and 75% of that is 9900.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: subjects chart, average English
stem: Same chart. What is the average number of students who chose English over the 6 years?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: subjects chart, share in 2011
stem:
Same chart. If the total number of students in the university was 20000 in 2011, what
percentage of students chose at least one subject?

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q28, gates in an LSI package
stem: The number of logic gates contained in a single LSI IC package is:
answer:
**(a) More than 100.** SSI has fewer than about 12 gates, MSI 12-99, LSI 100 to about
10000, VLSI more.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Q7, boat downstream
answer:
**(d) 54 minutes.** Upstream speed $= 90/(11/3) = 270/11 \approx 24.55$ km/h, so the
stream flows at $62 - 24.55 = 37.45$ km/h and downstream speed is $99.45$ km/h:
$90/99.45$ h $\approx 54.3$ minutes.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q22, 23 AND 23
stem: What is the decimal result of the AND operation on A = 23 and B = 23?

subject: C programming
topic: Functions, recursion, scope and storage classes
title: Q24, address of a register variable
stem: Which option is correct regarding the code snippet below?
answer:
**(a) Compile-time error at Line 1**: C forbids taking the address of a
`register` variable (GCC: "address of register variable requested"). (C++ allowed
it until C++17 removed `register`.)

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: Q21, binary to hexadecimal
stem: What is the hexadecimal equivalent of the binary number 11011011?

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q32, incorrect statement about stacks
stem: Which one of the given options is incorrect about stacks?
options: Balancing of symbols is one of the applications of stacks.
Stack is said to be in underflow state if it is empty.
Stacks can be implemented using both array and trees.
TOP equal to zero implies only one element in the stack.
answer:
**(c).** Stacks are implemented with arrays or linked lists, not trees. (With the
usual convention `top = -1` for an empty stack, `top == 0` does mean exactly one
element, so (d) is correct; popping an empty stack is underflow.)

subject: Verbal ability
topic: Vocabulary in context, definitions and spelling
title: word for a definition (19 items)
stem:
Choose the word that matches the definition.

1. unconquerable; unbeatable; invulnerable; indisputable - fortuitous, precarious,
    awry, impregnable
2. stretched tight - indomitable, robust, taut, proportionate
3. forward movement; progress; promotion - general, advancement, sign, meter
4. garland of flowers, leaves etc. hung between two points - glut, divisibility,
    festoon, demagogue
5. meticulously; exactly; scrupulously; diligently; thoroughly; in detail -
    minutely, approximately, obviously, especially
6. to publish; to distribute; to circulate; to come forth; to emit; to result from
    - issue, entrust, honor, prove
7. the act or state of lying concealed to surprise or attack the enemy - legging,
    deference, ambush, foreman
8. to implore - induct, underrate, disburden, beseech
9. unchangeable - invariable, mercenary, slothful, pestilential
10. doubtful; dubious - civic, suspect, duplicate, coordinate
11. against; in contrast to - curtly, contra, either, nevertheless
12. safety; protection; defense - security, career, import, advice
13. signed note acknowledging a debt - Inc., G.D.P., I.O.U., PTO
14. pertaining to spring - cadaverous, venerable, indefatigable, vernal
15. conclusion reached by reasoning from data or premises; speculation - candor,
    aristocracy, inference, raconteur
16. to create; to produce; to bring into being - acquire, generate, browse,
    dislodge
17. the practical unit of electric-current strength - epithet, rationalism,
    ampere, prepossession
18. absolute - subservient, similar, sheer, homogeneous
19. to annoy; to irritate - discourse, impugn, forbear, nettle
answer:
(1) impregnable, (2) taut, (3) advancement, (4) festoon, (5) minutely, (6) issue,
(7) ambush, (8) beseech, (9) invariable, (10) suspect, (11) contra, (12) security,
(13) I.O.U., (14) vernal, (15) inference, (16) generate, (17) ampere, (18) sheer
(as in "sheer nonsense"), (19) nettle.

One photo of item 5 shows "approximately" selected, which is the opposite of the
definition. In this format a wrong answer usually costs marks, so "?" is the safe
choice when unsure.

subject: Verbal ability
topic: Vocabulary in context, definitions and spelling
title: correct spelling (6 items)
stem:
Choose the right spelling: (1) merchandise / merchendise; (2) accidentally /
accidentelly; (3) indispensable / indispensible; (4) quarrel / quarrell; (5) acquisition /
aquisition; (6) indefatigable / indefatiguable.
answer:
(1) merchandise, (2) accidentally, (3) indispensable, (4) quarrel, (5) acquisition,
(6) indefatigable. (Some second spellings are blurred in the photos; the first form of
each pair is the correct one.)

subject: Verbal ability
title: fill the gap (8 items)
stem:
Choose the option that fills the gap.

1. There are times when you have to force yourself to improve your performance, and
    that's simply called self-___. - mastery, manifestation, movement, motivation
2. I am writing ___ you of my change of address. - for to inform, to informing,
    to inform, for informing
3. There was no fixed agenda for that particular day as it was to be regarded simply
    as a ___ meeting. - unplanned, casual, possible, probable
4. Thanks for your help. `___' - You're welcome., Never mind., It doesn't
    matter., Oh well.
5. If you want to try and influence that political party, it's best to become a member
    yourself and then you can argue from the ___. - beginning, side, inside, entrance
6. Feel free to visit anything of interest to you in the exhibition, and also, you can
    ___ of any of the refreshments available. - undertake, partake, retake, intake
7. What ___ of time would you stay with us if we offered you the job? - duration,
    long, length, span
8. She is very happy because she starts her new ___ today. - labour, worked,
    postponed, job
answer:
(1) motivation, (2) to inform, (3) casual, (4) You're welcome, (5) inside ("argue from
the inside"), (6) partake ("partake of" refreshments), (7) length ("what length of
time"; "duration" does not take "of time"), (8) job.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: A5, Max's rank
stem:
Smith is ranked 12th from the top and 20th from the bottom. If Max's rank is two positions
higher than Smith's, find Max's rank from the bottom.
answer:
**(b) 22nd.** There are $12 + 20 - 1 = 31$ students. Max is 10th from the top, so
$31 - 10 + 1 = 22$nd from the bottom.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: A7, five girls in a row
stem:
Five girls Q, S, R, T and U sit in a row facing north. U is second from the right end and
is adjacent to neither S nor R. The number of people between U and R equals the number
between Q and T. Who sits at the left end?
answer:
**(d) S.** With seats 1 to 5 from the left, U is in seat 4, so seats 3 and 5 hold Q
and T (one person, U, between them). One person must sit between U and R, so R is in seat
2 and S in seat 1.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: A9, Allen and Bob's brother
stem:
Introducing Allen, Bob said, "He is the father of my only brother's daughter's
daughter." How is Allen related to Bob's brother?
answer:
**(c) Son-in-law.** The father of the brother's daughter's daughter is the brother's
daughter's husband.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: C1, decreased by 12.5 per cent
stem: When a number is decreased by 12.5%, the result is 56. What is the original number?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: C2, selling price for 20 per cent profit
stem:
A retailer bought 100 artifacts for \$7000 and paid an extra \$500 in transportation.
What should the selling price of each artifact be to make a 20% profit?
answer: **\$90**: total cost 7500, with 20% profit 9000, i.e. 90 per artifact.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: C3, round trip at twice the speed
stem:
Alex drove from city P to city Q in $y$ hours. On the return trip his average speed was
twice as fast. What is the total driving time for the round trip?
answer: \textbf{$1.5y$ hours}: the same distance at twice the speed takes $y/2$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: C4, tallest boy at an end
stem:
In how many ways can five boys A to E, of different heights, be seated in a row so that the
tallest boy is at one of the ends?
answer: **48**: 2 choices of end for the tallest boy, then $4! = 24$ arrangements of the rest.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: C5, salaries in the ratio 4 to 5
stem:
The salaries of P and Q are in the ratio 4:5. If P gets a 25% increment, his salary
becomes \$1500. What is Q's current salary?

subject: Verbal ability
title: D3, rearrange, world hunger
stem:
Rearrange (1 and 6 fixed): 1. I wish we could - (A) so that no one (B) to end world
hunger (C) have enough money (D) in the entire world - 6. has to be hungry ever again.
answer:
**CBDA**: "I wish we could have enough money to end world hunger in the entire world
so that no one has to be hungry ever again."

subject: Verbal ability
title: D5, rearrange, the ocean
stem:
Rearrange (1 and 6 fixed): 1. As the - A. exuded a raw, untamed beauty that left
onlookers B. sprays of salty mist into the air, the coastal landscape C. waves crashed
against the rugged cliffs, sending D. in awe of the immense power and majesty of - 6. the
ocean.
answer:
**CBAD**: "As the waves crashed against the rugged cliffs, sending sprays of salty
mist into the air, the coastal landscape exuded a raw, untamed beauty that left onlookers
in awe of the immense power and majesty of the ocean."

subject: Verbal ability
title: D1, fill in, much ... with the change
stem:
Fill in the blank: She was much _____ with the change in his behaviour. (The options
are off screen.)
answer:
An adjective that takes "with": **pleased** (or "impressed", "annoyed"); "much"
before a past participle is idiomatic ("much pleased").

subject: Verbal ability
title: D9, gift-giving, psychologists and economists
stem:
(Reading comprehension, summarised: people spend billions every month on gifts; social
psychologists see gift-giving as a positive social tradition, while economists see it as a
waste of resources, the "deadweight loss" of gifts the recipient would not buy for
themselves.) What does the passage suggest about the relationship between social
psychologists and economists regarding gift-giving?
options: They collaborate to analyse the economic impact.
They unanimously agree on the benefits.
They jointly advocate for stricter rules during festive seasons.
They diverge in their viewpoints, with economists embracing doubt.
answer:
**(d).** The passage contrasts the two views ("economists hold a different
opinion"). The other options are not supported.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M1, Reynolds number
stem: What is the Reynolds number, and what does it indicate about the flow of a fluid?
options: It is the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces; it indicates whether the flow is laminar or turbulent.
It is the ratio of pressure forces to viscous forces; it indicates heat transfer in the fluid.
It is the ratio of gravitational forces to viscous forces; it indicates the density of the fluid.
It is the ratio of the velocity of sound to the flow velocity; it indicates the compressibility of the fluid.
answer:
**(a).** $Re = \rho v L / \mu$, inertial over viscous forces; low $Re$ means laminar,
high means turbulent (pipe flow transitions around 2300). The last option describes the
Mach number, inverted.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M3, pump versus compressor
stem:
What is the main difference between a pump and a compressor? (The option texts are cut off
on the right.)
answer:
A **pump** moves and pressurises an (essentially incompressible) liquid; a
**compressor** raises the pressure of a gas by reducing its volume. The intended
option is the one saying "a pump raises the pressure of a liquid, a compressor of a
gas".

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M4, mechanical advantage 5
stem:
A machine is designed to lift a load of 500 N. If its mechanical advantage is 5, what force
must be applied?

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M7, bottles and caps
stem:
For a project manufacturing cold-drink bottles, _____ is used for the bottles while
_____ is used for the caps.
answer:
**(b).** Hollow thin-walled bottles are blow moulded; small precise caps with threads
are injection moulded.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M8, not a machining operation
stem:
Which one of the operations is not part of machining, where raw material is converted to
the final shape by removing material?
answer: **(d) Molding**: it shapes material in a mould without removing any.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M9, statements about CNC machines
stem:
Which statements about CNC machines are correct? A. CNC stands for Computer Numerical
Control. B. A stepper motor is used as a drive unit. C. The accuracy of machinery is slightly
less than NC machines. D. A mini computer is used for the generation of the program in the
form of a file.
answer:
**(a) A & D only.** C is false: CNC is *more* accurate than NC. Among the
offered pairs only A & D avoids C. (B is also true in practice, since stepper or servo
motors drive the axes, but no option contains it without C.)

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M10, ore melted into two liquid layers
stem:
In which process are all components of an ore or concentrate completely melted and
separated into two liquid layers?
answer:
**(b) Smelting**: the charge melts and separates into a metal (or matte) layer and a
slag layer.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M11, hardness test of mineralogists
stem: Which hardness test is preferred by mineralogists to help identify minerals?
answer: **(c) Scratch hardness** (the Mohs scale): which mineral scratches which.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M13, heat removed per unit work
stem: What is the ratio of useful heat removed to the work done in a refrigeration system called?
answer: **(b) Coefficient of performance**, $\mathrm{COP} = Q_L / W$.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M14, efficiency of a heat engine
stem:
A heat engine takes in 100 J and does 40 J of useful work; the remaining 60 J is lost. How
efficient is the engine?

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M15, gas from a cylinder feels cold
stem: Why does the stream of gas coming out of a pressurised cylinder feel cold?
options: Because the moisture present in the cylinder condenses
Because work is being done at the expense of thermal energy
Because the gas in the cylinder is thermally insulated
Because the velocity of the gas is high
answer:
**(b).** The expanding gas does work (adiabatically, too fast for heat to flow in),
so its internal energy and temperature fall.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M16, U-tube manometer
stem:
A U-tube partly filled with water is connected to a gas supply. The height difference
between the arms is 30 cm and the gas pressure in the tube is 10 kPa. What is the pressure
of the gas supply? ($g = 9.81$, water density 998 kg/m^3.)
answer:
**(a) 12.937 kPa** $= 10 + 998 \times 9.81 \times 0.30 / 1000$. The question says
"absolute", but the numbers only work as a gauge reading; adding the atmosphere would give
about 114 kPa, which is not an option.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M17, outflow from a 4 m tank
stem:
A tank of height 4 m is filled with a fluid of density 1000 kg/m^3. A hole
is opened at the bottom. What is the speed of the fluid leaving the tank?
answer:
**(b) 8.86 m/s**, by Torricelli: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 4}$. The
density does not matter.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M18, torque on a 25 mm shaft
stem:
A shaft of diameter 25 mm is subjected to a torsional shear stress of 80 MPa. What is the
maximum torque it can withstand?
answer:
$T = \pi d^3 \tau / 16 = 245\,437$ N mm $= 245.4$ N m, i.e. **(c)**. The option
"245.436 N-mm" has the right digits but the wrong unit (it is off by 1000).

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M19, gear speeds
stem:
A 20-tooth gear meshes with a 50-tooth gear. If the smaller gear turns at 1000 rpm, what is
the speed of the larger one?

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M20, exponential failure
stem:
A bulb has a constant failure rate of 0.004 per hour. Find the probability of failure within
250 hours and the MTTF, assuming an exponential distribution.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: M21, production plan for maximum profit
stem:
Part A needs 3 h of division X and 2 h of division Y; part B needs 2 h of X and 1 h of Y.
Profits are INR 5000 (A) and 3000 (B). X and Y have 20 and 12 hours a day. Which daily
targets maximise profit?
options: 4 units of A and 3 units of B
3 units of A and 4 units of B
4 units of A and 4 units of B
0 units of A and 10 units of B
answer:
**(c) 4 A and 4 B**: it uses exactly 20 h of X and 12 h of Y, with profit 32000,
the best over all integer plans (checked by enumeration). (d) gives 30000.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M22, radius of a beam in bending
stem:
A circular bar on a simple span carries a central load. Find its radius if the permissible
stress is 150 N/mm^2 and the maximum bending moment is 750 000 N mm.
answer:
$\sigma = 32M/(\pi d^3)$ gives $d = \sqrt[3]{32 \cdot 750000/(150\pi)} = 37.1$ mm, so the
**radius is about 18.5 mm: (a)**. The photo has 37 mm selected, which is the
*diameter*.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M24, cost of heating a room
stem:
An insulated room $5 \times 8 \times 4$ m is heated from 10 °C to 30 °C by a 1 kW heater
with 80% efficiency; no air leaves. Electricity costs ₹10 per kWh. Find the cost
($c_v$ of air $= 0.75$ kJ/kg K, density 1.25 kg/m^3).
answer:
**(b) ₹10.43.** Mass $= 160 \times 1.25 = 200$ kg; heat $= 200 \times 0.75 \times 20
= 3000$ kJ $= 0.833$ kWh; electricity $= 0.833/0.8 = 1.042$ kWh, so the cost is 10.42.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M27, connecting rod buckling
stem:
For a connecting rod to buckle equally about the X and Y axes (the Y-axis along the longer
length of the cross-section), what should the relation between the moments of inertia be?
answer:
\textbf{(c) $I_{xx} = 4 I_{yy}$.} About one axis the rod buckles as pin-ended (length
$L$); about the other its ends are effectively fixed (length $L/2$). Equal Euler loads
need $I/L_e^2$ equal, i.e. a factor of 4.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M28, material removal rate in drilling
stem:
A 7 mm drill runs at 1000 rpm with a penetration rate of 1 mm/min. Calculate the material
removal rate.
answer:
$\mathrm{MRR} = (\pi d^2/4) \times \text{feed rate} = 38.5$ mm^3/min
$= 3.85 \times 10^{-8}$ m^3/min, so **(d)** by its digits. The
options' exponent is wrong (or the feed was meant to be 1 m/min); the spindle speed is not
needed when the penetration rate is given.

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M29, hollow pipe as a beam
stem:
A hollow steel pipe with moment of inertia 267 035 mm^4 is a simply
supported beam of span 1.5 m. With a permissible stress of 150 N/mm^2,
what concentrated load can it carry at mid-span?

subject: Other
topic: Mechanical engineering (thermodynamics, fluids, strength of materials, manufacturing)
title: M30, heated tube length for mercury
stem:
Liquid mercury flows at 1.5 kg/s through a 30 mm tube, entering at 20 °C and leaving at
40 °C. The wall is held at 50 °C, $h = 4200$ W/m^2 °C and
$c_p = 140$ J/kg °C. What is the approximate tube length for constant heat flux?
answer:
**(a) 0.5 m.** $Q = \dot m c_p \Delta T = 1.5 \times 140 \times 20 = 4200$ W. Using the
wall-to-outlet difference $50 - 30$ (mean bulk temperature 30 °C):
$L = Q/(h \pi d \Delta T) = 4200/(4200 \pi \cdot 0.03 \cdot 20) = 0.53$ m.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: only graduates are eligible
stem:
Choose the most logical option. If only graduates are eligible for this job, and some
applicants are not graduates, then "some applicants are not eligible for this job":
options: may or may not be true
answer: **(a) Always true**: the applicants who are not graduates are not eligible.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: geniuses and conformists
stem:
No genius is a conformist. Creative people are never conformists. Conclusion: therefore,
all creative people are geniuses.
answer:
**(b) Invalid.** Both groups avoid conformity, but that says nothing about creative
people being geniuses (two subsets of the same complement may be disjoint).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: simple versus compound interest
stem:
A sum is invested at 8% simple interest and the same sum at 10% compound interest
(annually). The difference between the interests after 2 years is Rs. 128. The sum is:
answer:
**None of the options as printed.** CI $- $ SI $= P(0.21 - 0.16) = 0.05P = 128$ gives
$P = 2560$. The question is probably garbled (for example, with 10% for both rates the
difference would be $0.01P$ and $P = 12800$, option (b)).

subject: Logical reasoning
title: course of action for low marks
stem:
Situation: a student is consistently getting low marks in mathematics. Courses of action:
(1) The student should be provided with extra tutoring or special classes. (2) The student
should be advised to stop studying mathematics altogether.
answer: **(a) Only 1**: it addresses the problem; abandoning the subject does not.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: partition exchange sort
stem: Which sorting technique is also known as partition exchange sort?
answer:
**(a) Quick sort.** (The question also calls it "stable"; quicksort is not stable,
but it is the algorithm known as partition-exchange sort.)

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: decrease in car sales 2006 to 2008
stem:
A bar chart shows car sales by year (2006: 40000, 2008: 25000, as far as the photo shows).
What is the percentage decrease from 2006 to 2008?
answer: **(b) 37.5%** $= 15000/40000$, with the values read from the bars.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
topic: Recursion, backtracking and divide and conquer
title: call stack with tail-call optimisation
stem:
$f(n)$ returns the factorial of $n$ and is tail-recursive. If the compiler optimises tail
recursion, what is the maximum depth of the call stack at any time for $f(10)$?
answer: **(c) 1**: tail-call optimisation reuses the current frame for each recursive call.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: inserting into a circular linked list
stem: Insertion of a node in a circular linked list requires modification of at least:
answer: **(b) 2 pointers**: the new node's `next` and its predecessor's `next`.

subject: Mathematics
title: set difference
answer: \textbf{(b) $\{8, 26, 36, 79\}$}: the elements of $A$ not in $B$.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: nodes of a full binary tree
stem: If a full binary tree has 10 leaf nodes, what is the total number of nodes?
answer: **(a) 19**: a full binary tree with $L$ leaves has $L - 1$ internal nodes.

subject: Java
topic: Algorithms and output prediction in Java
title: Newton iteration in Java
stem:
What is the output? `SomeFunction(16)` starts with `result = number / 2` and
repeats `temp = result; result = (temp + number / temp) / 2;` while
`(temp - result) != 0`, then returns `result`; `main` prints it.
answer:
**4** (printed as `4.0`): this is Newton's method for $\sqrt{16}$; from 8 it goes
5, 4.1, 4.001, ..., and stops when two iterates are exactly equal at 4.0.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: height of a binary tree
stem:
What does the program print? `height(root)` returns 0 for `null` and otherwise
$1 + \max$ of the children's heights; the tree has root 15, children 10 and 20, and
grandchildren 8, 12, 16, 25 (one candidate's version uses slightly different values).
answer: **3**: three levels of nodes.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: worst case of selection sort
stem: Ten people's ages are sorted with selection sort. What is the worst-case complexity?
answer: \textbf{$O(n^2)$}: selection sort always scans the unsorted part, in every case.

subject: Java
topic: Algorithms and output prediction in Java
title: output of a bubble sort
stem:
`arr = {11, 9, 10, 45, 22}` is passed to a function that does a standard bubble sort
in place; then the elements are printed. What is the output?
answer: **9 10 11 22 45**: Java passes the array reference, so the caller sees it sorted.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: no value in the first 5 slots
stem:
Five values are inserted into a hash table of size 20 with chaining. If hashing is uniform,
what is the probability that no value is stored in the first 5 slots?
answer:
\textbf{$(15/20)^5$}: each value independently avoids the first 5 slots with probability
$15/20$; with chaining, slots can be reused, so the factors do not decrease.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: pocket money
stem:
Jia spends 20% of her pocket money $X$ on necessary purchases and 5% of the remainder on
transport, and is left with Rs. 1520. What is $X$?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a rectangular plot
stem:
The length of a rectangular plot is increased by 10%. By what percent must the breadth be
decreased to keep the area the same?
answer: **100/11%**: the breadth becomes $1/1.1 = 10/11$ of itself, a decrease of $1/11$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a hexagonal table
stem:
Adam, Abe, Pepa, Jill, Bob and Ron sit at the corners of a hexagonal table facing the centre.
Adam is second to the left of Ron; Abe is a neighbour of Pepa and Jill; Bob is second to the
left of Jill. Who sits opposite Adam?
answer:
**Jill** (checked by enumerating all seatings, with either reading of "left"; the
`sol.txt` key agrees). The NIT candidate's sheet says Pepa, which is wrong.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: an energy-drink argument
stem:
50 consumers were given a brand's herbal energy drink in time-bound situations and 80% said
it helped their productivity; "hence it is the best energy drink in the market". The
argument is most vulnerable because it fails to consider:
options: that some participants were allergic to herbs
that the herbs are not harmful
that the price of the drink is high
whether the consumers had tasted other brands
answer:
**(d).** "Best in the market" is a comparison, and the study never compared the drink
with any other brand.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: cats, dogs, frogs, bats
stem:
Some cats are dogs. No dog is a frog. All frogs are bats. Some bats are eagles.
Conclusions: (1) Some frogs are not eagles. (2) No dog is a bat. (3) Some cats are bats.
(4) No eagle is a cat.
answer:
**No conclusion follows.** Each conclusion is possible but none is forced (frogs may all
be eagles, dogs may be bats that are not frogs, and so on). The NIT candidate's "only 1" is
wrong.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: drip irrigation
stem:
Gardener: install drip irrigation besides the sprinklers, so the lawns do not dry out if
someone forgets to water them; this costs less than redoing damaged lawns. Owner: it is
expensive and unnecessary. Which choice best supports the gardener?
options: The use of sprinklers can still reduce the longevity of the lawns due to underwatering
Severe rains can rot the lawns
Snow storms can damage the lawns
Drip irrigation can save the lawns when nobody is there to water them
answer:
**(a)** \unverified. It answers "unnecessary": sprinklers alone still allow the costly
underwatering damage. (d) merely restates the gardener's claim.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: five students in a row
stem:
A and B are adjacent; C and D are adjacent; A is not next to E, who is at the left end; B is
second from the right; C is to the right of both D and E; B and C are together.
Conclusions: (1) B is between C and A. (2) A is between C and B.
answer: **Only (2) is incorrect.** The only order is E D C B A (checked by enumeration).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a mocktail
stem:
15 litres hold water and mocktail mix in the ratio $10 : 5$. What fraction of the mixture
must be drawn out and replaced by mix to make it half and half?
answer:
**1/4**: removing $x$ litres leaves $10 - \tfrac23 x$ water; $= 7.5$ gives $x = 3.75$,
a quarter of 15. (The NIT candidate's 1/3 is wrong.)

subject: Logical reasoning
title: enough fuel for 600 miles?
stem:
A bus with a full tank of unknown size and efficiency must go 600 miles. (1) The driver drives
at constant speed. (2) After 150 miles, three quarters of the tank is left. (3) After 450
miles, three quarters of the tank is left. Which statements suffice?
answer:
**1 and 2, or 1 and 3** (the key agrees). At constant consumption either measurement
gives the range (600 or 1800 miles).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: mixing rice
stem:
Bob mixes rice R1 and R2 in the ratio $4 : 7$ and sells at Rs. 17/kg at a 15% loss. R2
costs Rs. 22/kg. What does R1 cost?
answer: **Rs. 16.5**: the mixture costs $17/0.85 = 20$, so $4x + 7 \cdot 22 = 220$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a perfume's stock
stem:
A perfume launched in March 1997 sells $2/7$ of the stock at the start of each year by 31
December. In which year does the stock fall below $1/4$ of the original?
answer:
**2001**: $(5/7)^4 \approx 0.26$ at the end of 2000 and $(5/7)^5 \approx 0.19$ at the end
of 2001 (the key agrees).

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a calendar
stem: 21 August 1995 was a Monday, and 1996 was a leap year. What day was 24 August 1998?
answer:
**Monday**: $1 + 2 + 1 + 1$ odd days for 1996-98 plus 3 days $= 8 \equiv 1$...\
counted exactly, 1098 days $= 156$ weeks $+ 6$, and $+3$ more days gives Monday (checked with
a calendar library).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: exactly one fudge ball
stem:
A box has 4 caramel twists, 3 truffles and 2 fudge balls. John picks 3 pieces. Probability of
exactly one fudge ball?
answer: **1/2** $= \binom21\binom72/\binom93 = 42/84$. (The NIT candidate's 1/4 is wrong.)

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a strange subtraction
answer:
**1** \unverified. The true differences are 6, 16, 24 and the results are the squares of
their tens digits (0, 1, 4); $42 - 28 = 14$ gives $1^2 = 1$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: truth-tellers in a chess club
stem:
Teams T1, T2, T3: one always tells the truth, one always lies, one alternates. They meet on
Tuesday, Friday and Sunday, each team preferring a different day. T1: "Tuesday is the most
comfortable day and Friday is comfortable for T2." T2: "Friday is comfortable for T3 and
Sunday for T1." T3: "Tuesday is the most comfortable day and T1 is comfortable with
Sunday." Which team tells the truth?
answer:
**T2.** Brute force over all day and type assignments gives exactly one solution: T1
Sunday (liar), T2 Tuesday (truth), T3 Friday (alternates).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: pounds bought and sold
stem:
A graph gives US dollars per pound for a week: Sun 1.75, Mon 1.75, Tue 1.70, Wed 1.75, Thu
1.70, Fri 1.70, Sat 1.65, Sun 1.60. Mrs Lindsay buys 200 pounds on Tuesday and sells them on
Wednesday. Her profit in dollars?
answer: **\$10** $= 200 \times 0.05$ (the Apti-2 key agrees).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: dollar against euro
stem:
With the dollar graph above and euros per pound 1.40, 1.35, 1.35, 1.30, 1.35, 1.30, 1.25, 1.20
over the same days, by how much did the dollar depreciate against the euro over the week?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: arranging books
stem:
B1 is 24th from the left and B2 is 27th from the right; only B3 lies between them. Minimum
number of books?
answer: **48**: put B2 left of B1, at position 22; the shelf needs $22 + 27 - 1 = 48$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: grids with a missing value
answer:
**10** \unverified. In B each edge number is the sum of its two corners and the centre
($4 + 5 + 4 = 13$, $5 + 6 + 4 = 15$, $2 + 6 + 4 = 12$), so $? = 4 + 2 + 4$. Grid A does not
follow this rule cleanly, so the intended rule is uncertain.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: gym members
stem:
A bar graph shows members of gyms A and B in 1990-94 (1994: A 70, B 150). If 1995 has 30%
more members in total than 1994, how many?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a pie chart
stem:
A pie chart splits 160000 as Hemant 15%, Dharam 10%, Chandru 15%, Abir 25%, Bhanu 35%.
By what percent does Chandru's share exceed Dharam's?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a row of parked vehicles
stem:
V1 is 20th to the left of V2, which is 27th from the right; V3 is 19th from the left and 11th
to the right of V1. How many vehicles?
answer: **54**: V1 is 8th from the left, V2 is 28th, and $28 + 27 - 1 = 54$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: meal-prep techniques (variant)
stem:
T1 is twice as effective as T4 but less than T5; T2 is thrice T5; T3 equals T4. Conclusions:
(1) $T5 \ge T1$, (2) $T2 > T5$, (3) $T2 > T1$, (4) $T4 > T1$.
answer:
(1), (2) and (3) all follow and (4) does not, so no option is exact \unverified; the Apti-2
key writes "1&2 or 1&3".

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a syllogism about tapioca
stem:
Statements: (A) No plant root is edible. (B) Tapioca is not edible. (C) Tapioca is edible.
(D) Tapioca is not a plant root. (E) Tapioca is a stem. Which three form a valid argument?
answer: **ACD**: no plant root is edible, tapioca is edible, so tapioca is not a plant root.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: cookie teams
stem:
Teams of 3 sell cookies. Did some member sell at least 2 boxes? (1) The team sold 6 in total.
(2) All three sold different numbers.
answer:
**Either statement alone suffices**: (1) by pigeonhole ($6/3 = 2$); (2) three distinct
non-negative numbers have a maximum of at least 2.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a strange multiplication
answer:
**3**: the result is the difference of the two numbers' digit differences:
$|0 - 2| = 2$, $|1 - 6| = 5$, $|1 - 0| = 1$, so $|1 - 4| = 3$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: sweet shop table
stem:
A table gives the marked price, discount and profit of sweets. Ras Malai's cost equals
Rasgulla's (Rasgulla: marked price $1.25\times$ cost, 8% discount, profit Rs. 48); Ras Malai
is marked at $1.5625\times$ cost and sold at a 20% discount. Profit on Ras Malai?
answer:
**80.** Rasgulla: $1.25 \times 0.92 = 1.15$, so cost $= 48/0.15 = 320$. Ras Malai sells
at $320 \times 1.5625 \times 0.8 = 400$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a bakery's stock
stem:
Three items are in the ratio $2 : 3 : 4$ in 2020. Removing $X$ of each gives $3 : 5 : 7$ in
2021; removing 10 more of each gives $1 : 2 : 3$ in 2022. Total removed in 2021?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: did Jamie pay more?
stem:
John bought a TV in a sale for Rs. 15000 and sold it to Jamie. Which statements tell whether
John made a profit? (I) Jamie sold it to Jake for 20000. (II) Jamie got a 20% discount on
John's marked price. (III) John's tag said 25000.
answer: **II and III together**: Jamie paid $0.8 \times 25000 = 20000 > 15000$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: meal-prep techniques
stem:
T1 is twice as effective as T4 but less effective than T5; T2 is thrice T5; T3 equals T4.
Conclusions: (1) T5 is the most effective. (2) T4 and T5 are the least. (3) T2 is the most.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a die's bar graph
stem:
A bar graph gives 20 rolls of a red die: 1 seven times, 2 eight times, 3, 5 and 6 once each and
4 twice. Estimate the mean roll.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: will the mean go up?
stem:
With the same bar graph (the white die was rolled 19 times: 3, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3 of the faces 1-6)
and the white die fair, what is the probability that the mean score increases after one more
roll?
answer:
**2/3** \unverified. The overall mean of the 39 rolls is $111/39 \approx 2.85$, so the
next roll must be 3 or more ... strictly 4, 5, 6 or a 3 (above 2.85): 4 faces of 6.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: mall elevators
stem:
Elevators E1, E3, E5 stop at even floors and E2, E4 at odd floors; all stop at the first and
seventh floors. Which must be true? (1) From the ground floor, E1 cannot take you to the fifth
floor. (2) From the sixth floor, E3 cannot take you to the ninth. (3) Going from an even floor
to an odd floor needs a change of elevator. (4) None of these.
answer:
**(4) None** \unverified: E1 stops at 7, so an even-to-odd trip is possible without
changing, and (1), (2) are only true for a direct ride. The IISc candidate's (3) is wrong.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: capacity of a pool
stem:
Pipes P1 and P2 fill a pool in 10 and 20 minutes; P3 drains 12 gallons per minute. Together
they fill it in 30 minutes. Capacity to the nearest integer?

subject: Logical reasoning
title: a row of athletes
stem:
In a row of 30 facing north, A1 is 13th from the left and 6th to the right of A2. A2's
position from the right?
answer: **24th**: A2 is 7th from the left, so $30 - 7 + 1 = 24$.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Zoey's age
stem:
Zoey's age in 2050? (I) When Zoey was born her father was 32, four years older than her
mother. (II) Her mother was born in the first leap year after 1970.
answer:
**Both together**: the mother was born in 1972 and was 28 at Zoey's birth (2000), so Zoey
is 50 in 2050.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: rearranging JUDGEMENT
stem: In how many arrangements of JUDGEMENT is J between the two Es?
answer:
**60,480**: choose 3 places for E, J, E ($\binom93$, one order) and arrange the other 6
letters ($6!$).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: a reading schedule
stem:
Monica reads 12 books of 260, 120, 115, 170, 165, 60, 200, 80, 155, 95, 105, 300 pages in
order, 60 pages a day, never starting a new book on the day she finishes one. How many books
are finished at the end of day 32? (Options not in the source.)
answer:
**11**: each book takes $\lceil p/60 \rceil$ days: 5, 2, 2, 3, 3, 1, 4, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, with
running totals ..., 27, 29, 34; the 11th book ends on day 29.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: alphanumeric series
stem: Next term: KM10, PR15, UW20, XZ23, ...
answer:
**CE2**: the number is the first letter's position minus 1 (K = 11, P = 16, U = 21, X =
24), and the next first letter is C (3). The BHU candidate's CE22 is wrong.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: grids A and B
answer:
**10**: the middle is (product of the digits on the left) $-$ (product on the right):
$15 - 12$, $20 - 3$, $27 - 6$; in B, $12 - 2 = 10$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: barks and meows
stem:
A dog barks every 2 minutes and a cat meows every 5 minutes. In 24 hours the barks exceed the
meows by about what percent?
answer: **150%**: 720 barks against 288 meows.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: encoding words
stem: Annual is encoded ESTKIU and Quarter UZGYJNJ. Encode Week.
answer:
**IJKR**: the $i$th letter is shifted by $i + 3$ (W$+4$, E$+5$, E$+6$, K$+7$) \unverified;
the given examples are not fully consistent at the wrap-around.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: father and son
stem:
Two years ago X was six times his son's age; in two years twice X's age will be seven times
the son's. Ratio of present ages?
answer: **13 : 3**: the son is 6 and X is 26.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: counting triangles
stem:
How many triangles are in the figure (a rectangle with a zig-zag line between its long sides
and one long diagonal)?
answer:
**22**, counted by computer from the figure's line segments (every triple of pairwise
intersecting segments with three distinct intersection points). The IISc candidate's 25 is
wrong.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: counting triangles (another figure)
stem:
How many triangles are in the figure (a tall rectangle cut into halves, crossing lines and
four small rectangles)?
answer: \unverified{} The photo is too skewed to count reliably; the candidate's sheet says 21.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: max of row minima
stem: For an $n \times n$ matrix, find each row's minimum and then the largest of them. Time?
answer: \textbf{$O(n^2)$}: every entry is read once.

subject: Operating systems
title: preventing deadlocks
stem:
A: Permitting resource preemption alone will prevent deadlocks. B: Preventing circular wait
alone will prevent deadlocks.
answer:
**Both true** \unverified: breaking any one of the four Coffman conditions prevents
deadlock. (Many keys say "A false, B true", because preemption is impractical for resources
such as printers.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: reversing an array
answer: **Both true.**

subject: C programming
title: size of a struct array
answer:
**120** (tested with 4-byte pointers): 12 bytes per struct. The candidates' 160 and 200
are wrong.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: sign-magnitude
stem: The sign-magnitude representation of $-15$ is:
answer: **11111**: sign bit 1 followed by $15 = 1111$.

subject: Operating systems
title: fixed partitions
stem:
Fixed partitions 600, 200, 100, 500 (from the diagram); three processes of 200 each are placed
by first fit. Ratio of internal to external fragmentation?
answer:
\unverified{} First fit uses 600, 200 and 500, wasting $400 + 0 + 300 = 700$ inside
partitions; the 100 partition stays free. No option matches the textbook definitions; the
candidate chose 1:1.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: counting print calls
answer: \textbf{$(n^2 - n)/2$}: one call per pair $i < j$.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: printing a circular list
answer: \textbf{$O(1)$}: one pointer.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: 8085 factorial
stem:
```c
MULTIPLY:      MOV E, B
               MVI A, 00H
MULTIPLYLOOP:  ADD D
               XXX
               MOV D, A
               RET
```

What replaces
XXX?
answer: **DCR E; JNZ MULTIPLYLOOP**: multiply D by B by adding D, E times.

subject: C programming
topic: Functions, recursion, scope and storage classes
title: a recursive power

subject: Logical reasoning
title: the oldest sister
stem:
P is younger than S and R is older than T. Who is oldest? (1) R is older than P. (2) S is
older than R. (3) T is the youngest.
answer: **Only 2**: $S > R > T$ and $S > P$ (the key agrees).

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: separated As
stem: How many 5-letter strings from A, A, B, M, T have the two As apart?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: two workers
stem:
A and B together finish in 7.5 days; A doing half and then B the other half takes 20 days. How
long does B alone take, if A is faster?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: tracking two vehicles
stem:

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: which implementation is fastest?
stem:
A cacheless processor has L1 RAM $>$ L2 RAM $>$ FLASH in speed; `.bss` and `.stack`
are in L1, `.data` and `.heap` in L2. `compute_sum` adds a range into (1) the

answer:
**(3) slowest, (2) fastest** (official solution). Here the static lives in
`.data` (L2) and is touched every iteration, while the local lives on the stack (L1).
\unverified: most compilers place a zero-initialised static in `.bss`.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: why the drain current saturates
stem:
The square-law model of an nMOS predicts a parabola, but in reality $I_D$ stays nearly
constant beyond $V_{DS} = V_{GS} - V_{TH}$. Why?
options: Some channel still exists even when $V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{TH}$
The channel is pinched off but current flows due to minority charge carriers
Past the pinch-off point, the electrons shoot through the depletion region near the drain junction and arrive at the drain terminal
$V_{DS}$ is so high that current flows from the bulk to the drain via the substrate
answer:
**(c).** After pinch-off the extra $V_{DS}$ falls across the short depletion region,
whose field sweeps the arriving electrons to the drain, so the current hardly changes.

subject: Embedded systems and electronics
title: rms current
stem:
A source $1\sin t$ V in series with 1 $\Omega$ feeds 1 $\Omega$ in parallel with a series 1 F
capacitor and 1 H inductor. The rms value of $i(t)$?
answer:
\textbf{$1/\sqrt2$ A.} At $\omega = 1$ the series LC branch has impedance
$j(\omega L - 1/\omega C) = 0$, so it shorts the parallel 1 $\Omega$. The source then sees
1 $\Omega$, $i = \sin t$, and the rms value is $1/\sqrt2$.

In two's complement, $+1 \to -1$ toggles every bit.

subject: Computer architecture and digital logic
title: setup or hold?
stem:
A D flip-flop's Q feeds back to D through a 0.2 ns delay; $T_{cq} = 1.5$ ns,
$T_{su} = 1$ ns, $T_h = 2$ ns, and CLK reaches it through CLK_BUF (delay 0). (A) Which
violation? (B) What CLK_BUF delay raises the frequency by 1.5$\times$?
options: A: hold violation; B: the CLK_BUF delay does not affect the frequency
A: no violation; B: the CLK_BUF delay does not affect the frequency
answer:
**(b).** The new data arrive $T_{cq} + 0.2 = 1.7$ ns after the edge, earlier than
$T_h = 2$ ns, so this is a hold violation. With one flip-flop, launch and capture use the same
buffered clock, so the buffer delay cancels and cannot change the frequency.

options: In push operation, if new nodes are inserted at the beginning of the linked list, then in pop operation, nodes must be removed from the end.
In push operation, if new nodes are inserted at the end, then in pop operation, nodes must be removed from the beginning.

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q10, variables
stem: What are the entities whose values can be changed called?
answer: **(b) Variables.**

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q11, merge sort on sorted input
stem: What is the time complexity of running merge sort on an array that is already sorted?
answer:
\textbf{(a) $O(n \log n)$.} Standard merge sort always splits down to single elements and
merges every level, regardless of the input order. (Natural merge sort or Timsort would
detect the single run and take $O(n)$, but that is not plain merge sort.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q12, searching a sorted list
stem:
Given a sorted list of items, which search algorithm would you choose to search for an item
most efficiently?
answer: **(d) Binary search**, $O(\log n)$ on a sorted array.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q13, postorder from inorder and preorder
stem:
The inorder and preorder traversals of a binary tree are `d b e a f c g` and
`a b d e c f g`. What is the postorder traversal?
options: e d b g f c a
d e b f g c a
e d b f g c a
d e f g b c a
answer:
**(b) `d e b f g c a`.** Preorder gives the root `a`; inorder splits it into
left $\{d, b, e\}$ and right $\{f, c, g\}$. Recursively the left subtree is `b` with
children `d, e`, and the right is `c` with children `f, g`: a perfect tree of
height 2, whose postorder is left-right-root.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q14, separate chaining worst case
stem: For hashing using separate chaining, what is the worst-case search time?
answer:
\textbf{(c) $O(n)$:} all $n$ keys can hash to the same bucket, making one long chain.
(Java 8's `HashMap` turns long chains into trees to get $O(\log n)$, but the textbook
chaining answer is $O(n)$.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q15, stack from queues
stem:
For a stack with $n$ elements, would it be unfeasible to implement stack operations on
queues in the case of a large dataset?
options: Yes, because of its time complexity $O(n)$
Yes, because of its time complexity $O(\log n)$
Yes, because extra memory is required
answer:
**(d) No, it should be feasible.** With two queues (or one, rotating), one of push or
pop costs $O(n)$ and the other $O(1)$ (amortised variants exist). That is slower than a
native stack but perfectly workable, and it needs only $O(n)$ memory, the same as the data.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q16, data structure for BFS
stem:
What data structure would you use to traverse a given graph using the breadth-first search
(BFS) algorithm?
answer: **(c) Queue.** BFS visits vertices in FIFO order of discovery; DFS uses a stack.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q17, storing score frequencies
stem:
A program $P$ reads 500 integers in the range $[0, 100]$, the scores of 500 students, and
then prints the frequency of each score above 50. What would be the best way for $P$ to
store the frequencies?
options: A dynamically allocated array of 550 numbers
answer:
**(a) An array of 50 numbers,** one counter for each score $51, 52, \dots, 100$. (The
last option is cut off in the photo; its number is read as 550, the usual wording of this
question.)

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q18, triple loop complexity

constants; only the middle loop depends on $n$: $10 \cdot n \cdot 6 = 60n$.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q19, sorted array operations
stem:
Given a sorted array of distinct items, which operation would result in a time complexity
of more than $O(1)$?
answer:
**(c) Deleting an element.** The $i$-th smallest is `a[i-1]` and the $i$-th
largest is `a[n-i]`, both $O(1)$; deleting needs shifting, $O(n)$.

subject: Java
title: Q20, constructor chain
stem: What is the output of the following code?
options: Person created Superhero created Batman created
Batman created Superhero created Person created
answer:
**(a).** Every constructor first calls its superclass constructor (an implicit
`super()`), so construction runs from the top of the hierarchy down.
(Compiled and run with `javac`/`java`.)

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q21, accessing private members
stem:
Given a class with only private data members, how would you access the members from an
object of the class?
options: Create public member functions to access those data members
Create private member functions to access those data members
Create protected member functions to access those data members
Private data members can never be accessed from outside the class
answer:
**(a)** public getters and setters. Private or protected functions are not callable
from outside the class either. (C++ `friend` functions and Java reflection are other
ways, but not among the options.)

subject: C++ and object-oriented programming
title: Q22, code reusability
stem: Which of the following object-oriented programming features describes code reusability?
answer: **(d) Inheritance:** a subclass reuses the fields and methods of its superclass.

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q23, hash table lookup
stem:
Which of the following does NOT impact how efficiently a lookup operation can be performed
in a hash table?
options: Number of buckets in the hash table
Number of elements stored in the hash table
Size of elements stored in the hash table
answer:
**(d) Size of the elements.** Lookup cost is governed by the load factor
(elements / buckets) and by how evenly the hash function spreads keys. How large each stored
value is does not change the number of probes (only, marginally, the cost of hashing and
comparing keys).

subject: Data structures and algorithms
title: Q25, linked list versus array
stem:
Which of the following points is/are true about the linked list data structure when
compared with an array?
options: It is easy to insert and delete elements in Linked List
Random access is not allowed in a typical implementation of Linked Lists
The size of array has to be pre-decided, linked lists can change their size any time.
answer:
**(d) All of the above.** Insertion and deletion at a known node are $O(1)$ (no
shifting), access by index needs a walk from the head, and nodes are allocated one at a
time, so the list grows and shrinks freely.

subject: Java
title: Q26, final method and a missing method
stem: What is the output of the following code?
answer:
**(c) Compiler error,** for two independent reasons: `Batman.greet()` tries to
override a `final` method, and `Superhero` has no method `show()`, so
`myHero.show()` does not compile. (`javac` reports both errors.)

title: sentence improvement
stem:

paying tribute to a* legend of music, Elvis Presley.
options: gathered there to paying tribute for the
gathered there for paying tribute for the
gathered there to pay tribute to the
answer:
**(c).** "To" + bare infinitive (*to pay*); the idiom is "pay tribute
*to*"; and "the legend" because Elvis is a specific person.

subject: Verbal ability
title: sentence improvement
stem:
Improve the part in italics: The most obvious downside to this pessimism is that
*it is coming at their expenses.*
options: it is costing at their expense
it will have came at their expense
it was coming at their expenses
answer:
**(a).** The idiom is "at someone's expense" (singular), and a general fact takes
the simple present.

subject: Verbal ability
title: sentence improvement
stem:
Improve the part in italics: *Many people of world keep* procrastinating and then
they lose in the end.
options: Many people in the world keeps
Many people in the world keep
answer:
**(c).** "In the world" needs the article, and the plural subject "many people"
takes "keep".

subject: Verbal ability
title: sentence improvement
stem: Improve the part in italics: A writer *always is having* his own vision of life.
answer:
**(a) always has.** "Have" in the sense of possess is a stative verb and does not
take the continuous form; the singular subject takes "has". (Also the option ticked
on screen.)

subject: Verbal ability
title: reading passage, "dissimulation"
stem:
(Passage summarised at the start of the chapter.) What is the contextual meaning of the
word "dissimulation" in the first line of the second paragraph ("bribe-takers and
bribe-payers have developed an elaborate theatre of dissimulation")?
answer:
**(a) Hypocrisy** (pretence, concealing one's real intentions): the next sentences
say the bribe is dressed up as some other kind of exchange. The screenshot ticks
*Clarity*, which is nearly the opposite.

subject: Verbal ability
title: reading passage, "obscurantist"
stem:
What is the contextual meaning of the word "obscurantist" (in "along with the
obscurantist language, bribe-taking culture ...")?

euphemisms and double meanings just described).

subject: Verbal ability
title: reading passage, attitude
stem: What best represents the author's attitude toward the rich in the West?
answer:
**(b) Mildly critical.** The author points out, with light irony, that rich
westerners do not see their own casual bribes (tipping for a restaurant table) as
corruption; there is no strong condemnation.

subject: Verbal ability
title: reading passage, inference
stem: What would the author most likely agree with?
options: People generally do not try to hide the money taken as bribe.
People hide the money taken as bribe primarily to avoid detection.
People hide the money taken as bribe from view even if detection possibility is low.
People hide the money taken as bribe to hide their economic background.
answer:
**(c).** The passage says avoiding a direct hand-over is common "even where there
is no chance of detection". (b) is explicitly only "one obvious reason".

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: hens and eggs
stem:
In a poultry farm, 50 hens give 200 eggs in 2 days. In how many days will 20 hens give
400 eggs?
answer:
**(b) 10.** One hen lays $200/(50 \cdot 2) = 2$ eggs a day, so 20 hens lay 40 a day
and need $400/40 = 10$ days.

$-3.4$ is a number on the real number line. If we subtract 1 from it, the new number will
be
options: Equally far from the origin as $-3.4$
answer: **(a).** $-4.4$ is 4.4 from the origin, farther than 3.4.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: selling cloth
stem:
A man bought 400 metres of cloth for Rs 40{,}000 and sold it at Rs 200 per one and a half
metres. What was his percentage profit or loss?
answer:
**(c) 33% profit.** Cost Rs 100 per metre; selling price $200/1.5 = 133.33$ per
metre, a profit of $33\tfrac13\%$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: proportional rectangle
stem:
The length and breadth of a rectangle are directly proportional. If the length increases
from 6 cm to 21 cm and the breadth is now 14 cm, what was the breadth before the
change?
answer:
**(a) 4 cm.** The ratio breadth : length is $14 : 21 = 2 : 3$, so the old breadth is
$6 \cdot \tfrac23 = 4$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: Alto owners
stem:
In a class of 80 students, $\tfrac45$ own cars. If $\tfrac{15}{16}$ of them own an Alto,
how many own an Alto?
answer: **(c) 60.** $\tfrac45 \cdot 80 = 64$ own cars and $\tfrac{15}{16} \cdot 64 = 60$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: remainder
stem: Find the remainder when $888\ldots8$ (the digit 8 repeated 63 times) is divided by 9.
answer:
**(c) 0.** A number is congruent to its digit sum mod 9: $8 \cdot 63 = 504$ and
$504 = 9 \cdot 56$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: buy one get one free
stem:
A shopkeeper offers "Buy 1, Get 1 Free" on a T-shirt marked at Rs 2{,}400. If after a
sale the shopkeeper earns a profit of 33.33%, what is the actual (cost) price of one
T-shirt?
answer:
**(a) Rs 900.** Two shirts are sold for 2400, which is $\tfrac43$ of their cost, so
two cost 1800 and one costs 900.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: divisibility by 30
stem:
The number $567xy$ is divisible by 30. The possible values of $x$ and $y$ respectively
can be
answer:
**(a) 0 and 0.** Divisible by 10 forces $y = 0$; divisible by 3 needs
$5 + 6 + 7 + x = 18 + x$ divisible by 3, so $x \in \{0, 3, 6, 9\}$. (Also the option
ticked on screen.)

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: cycling and walking
stem:
I started on my bicycle at 7 a.m. to reach a certain place. After some distance the
bicycle broke down; I rested for 35 minutes and walked all the way back home, reaching at
1 p.m. If my cycling speed is 10 km/h and walking speed 1 km/h, what distance did I
cover on the bicycle?
answer:
**(a) 4.92 km.** Moving time $= 6\,\text{h} - 35\,\text{min} = \tfrac{65}{12}$ h,
so $d/10 + d/1 = \tfrac{65}{12}$, $d = \tfrac{650}{132} \approx 4.92$.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: simple interest
stem:
Kriti invested an amount; at the end of 3 years it was worth Rs 4{,}960, and at the end of
another 5 years it was worth Rs 5{,}600. What is the rate of interest, if interest is
earned only on the principal?
answer:
**(c) 8%**, the intended answer, but only if "at the end of 5 years" means 5
years *from the start*: then 2 years earn 640, i.e. 320 a year, the principal is
$4960 - 3 \cdot 320 = 4000$ and the rate $320/4000 = 8\%$. Read literally (5 more
years, 8 in total), the interest is 128 a year, the principal 4576 and the rate 2.8%,
which is not an option.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: clock hands
stem: How many times in a day do the minute and hour hands of a clock cross each other?
answer:
**(d) 22.** The minute hand gains a full lap on the hour hand every $12/11$ hours,
so in 24 hours they meet $24 \cdot 11/12 = 22$ times (the overlap between 11 and 12
happens exactly at 12).

subject: Logical reasoning
title: university applications (1)
stem:
The graph shows the undergraduate applicants to Ralph University (thousands) and the
amount spent processing them (thousand \$):
|  | 2009 | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Applicants (000s) | 35 | 15 | 20 | 40 | 35 |
| Processing expenses (000s \$) | 4 | 8 | 5 | 3 | 9 |
Over the five years, on average, paper costs were 30% of the processing outlay, staff
salaries 45% and marketing 25%. Assume the revenue per applicant has not changed.

Select Yes if the statement is definitely true, otherwise No. *Statement:* In
2014, if the total number of applications is limited to 30{,}000 and processing costs
are held to \$5{,}000, the university will achieve a higher revenue total than in any of
the previous five years.
answer:
**No.** Revenue is (applicants) $\times$ (constant revenue per applicant), so
30{,}000 applicants give *less* revenue than 2009, 2012 or 2013. Holding costs down
affects profit, not revenue.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: university applications (2)
stem:
Same data as the previous question. Select Yes if the statement is definitely true,
otherwise No. *Statement:* Given the trend over the past five years, when the total
number of applicants increases, the cost of processing the applications decreases, and
vice versa.
answer:
**Yes** (as the test intends). Every year-on-year change moves the two series in
opposite directions: 2009-10 applicants down, cost up; 2010-11 up/down; 2011-12
up/down; 2012-13 down/up. (Whether a five-point trend is "definitely" a rule is
debatable, but the data never contradicts it.)

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Ethan's trips
stem:
Whenever Ethan drives a truck from Chicago to Michigan City, he also visits Old
St. Patrick's Church and Promontory Point Park. When he visits the church, he eats at the
bakery close to it; the bakery is famous in Michigan City for its blueberry cheesecake.
Ethan sometimes donates money to the church-run school. We also know that Ethan ate at the
bakery close to the church in June.

*Statement:* Ethan visited Old St. Patrick's Church in June. Is it definitely true,
could it be true, or can it not be true?
answer:
**Could be true.** "Church visit $\Rightarrow$ bakery" does not give
"bakery $\Rightarrow$ church visit": he may have eaten there without visiting the church.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: actors' obligations
stem:
Movie actors are bound by legal, ethical and contractual obligations to the movie's
investors: to be professional, finish the shoot on time, and not reveal details of the
movie without the director's consent. Any breach can lead to the actor being sued by the
production house, dismissed from the film, or having a long-term contract with the
production company rescinded. What inference can be drawn?
options: Both the actors' finances and their reputation will suffer if they breach their obligations.
Contractual penalties ensure that a production house does not have to enforce an actor's professional duties.
The severe penalties for breach of contract serve to deter actors from delaying the movie.
Actors are legally and contractually obligated to the movie's investors but not to the director or their fellow actors.
Lawsuits in the movie industry are mostly between production houses and the actors.
answer:
**(c)** \unverified. The passage lists finishing on time among the obligations and
describes heavy penalties, so a deterrent effect is the inference that stays closest to
the text. (a) adds "reputation", which is not mentioned; (b), (e) go beyond the text;
(d) is contradicted by the director's consent clause.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: strengthen the argument
stem:
"Five years ago I got a perfect score on the LSAT. Therefore I expect a perfect score
this time as well." Which statement, if true, most strengthens this claim?
options: Individual LSAT scores have been fairly consistent across multiple evaluations.
No new types of LSAT questions have been introduced in the past five years.
Five years ago, the LSAT was a paper-and-pencil test, and now it is an online test.
When I retook the GRE, my score was exactly the same as in my first attempt.
answer:
**(a).** It supports the hidden assumption that a person's LSAT score stays stable.
(b) helps a little; (c) weakens; (d) is about a different test.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: Sara's typing
stem:
Sara must type an email to a customer and some mathematical equations for a technical
manual. On average she types 35 words per minute and 2 equations per minute. The email
has at most 525 words (emails average 140 words). The manual has 5 sections, each
explaining at most 4 equations; the last manual had 3 equations per section.

Which statement has to be *definitely true* for Sara to commit to delivering the
typed email and equations within 21 minutes?
options: Introduction text of 150 words has to be copied and pasted from an existing email.
The email is written in points.
The length of the email is restricted to 450 words.
The technical manual has to be released with a lesser number of equations this year.
answer:
**(a).** Worst case now: $525/35 = 15$ minutes for the email plus
$20/2 = 10$ for the equations, 25 minutes. With 150 words pasted, at most 375 words are
typed: $10.7 + 10 = 20.7 \le 21$. With a 450-word limit it is still $12.9 + 10 = 22.9$;
(b) and (d) give no guaranteed bound.

subject: Logical reasoning
title: statement and assumption
stem:
*Statement:* "One of the main purposes of having a democratic society, run by
elected representatives, is to enable individuals to exercise freedom of expression."
*Assumption:* Freedom of expression is a benefit that the author of this statement
highly regards. Is the assumption implicit (Yes/No)?
answer:
**Yes.** Calling it one of the *main purposes* of democracy presupposes that
the author values it highly.

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: bank rates (2), Zeta index

Figure 2: the *Zeta index* $Z_{XY}$ of bank $X$ with respect to bank $Y$ is the
number of terms in which $X$ offers a higher rate than $Y$ (e.g. $Z_{AE} = 1$: only in

the rating of Bank J with respect to Bank G?

subject: Quantitative aptitude
title: branches and ATMs
stem:
Figure 1: branches and ATMs of ABC Bank by city category.
|  | 2011/12 | 2012/13 | 2013/14 |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Category | Branches | ATMs | Branches | ATMs | Branches | ATMs |
| A | 1,341 | 4,390 | 1,852 | 6,789 | 2,415 | 8,012 |
| B | 984 | 2,789 | 1,331 | 3,789 | 1,749 | 4,076 |
| C | 654 | 1,672 | 972 | 2,581 | 1,129 | 3,850 |
| D | 564 | 1,123 | 678 | 2,056 | 731 | 2,010 |
| E | 321 | 590 | 451 | 876 | 602 | 1,062 |
Figure 2 gives the average city population per category (A 120{,}000; B 75{,}000;
C 35{,}000; D 15{,}000; E 7{,}500) and Figure 3 the share of cities in 2013/14 (A 10%,
B 15%, C 20%, D 25%, E 30%). Which statement shows an *incorrect* analysis of
the trends during 2011-14?
options: The largest number of new branches and ATMs combined were opened in Category A cities.
The smallest number of new ATMs introduced were in Category E cities.
